Portfolio Case Study

A governed, multi-agent analytics engineering system.

Eight narrow-mandate agents that run a full analytics investigation end to end — hypothesis to stakeholder briefing — without bypassing the audit trail or the human sign-off that make the result trustworthy, and a ninth that invents new detection methods outside that chain. Built and validated against a synthetic, analytically rich fraud-and-abuse dataset.

In plain terms

Maldros does the core work of an analytics engineer — the person on a data team who turns messy business questions into trustworthy, quantified answers. Ask it something like “is this spike in API abuse coordinated fraud or just organic growth, and what is it costing us?” and it forms a hypothesis, pulls and analyzes the data, checks the statistics, has an internal “red team” try to poke holes in the conclusion, and writes up a plain-language briefing a non-technical executive can act on — all with safety checks wired into the pipeline that stop it from stating anything it cannot back up with a source, and that stop it from taking any consequential action until a human approves.

Today Maldros has been proven in a controlled simulation: one operator, a realistic but synthetic dataset that models fraud and abuse at an AI company, and jobs run one at a time. It is not running on any real company’s live data, and I am careful throughout never to imply otherwise. What it demonstrates is that an autonomous system can do this kind of analytical work at speed without giving up the things that make the work trustworthy — an audit trail, cited evidence for every claim, and a human holding final sign-off. If you take one idea from this document, take that one: the achievement is not that it is fast, it is that the speed costs nothing in accountability.

How to read this

I will not describe Maldros as more finished than it is, so every capability claim carries one of a small set of maturity labels, used consistently:

  • Validated via simulation / [Measured] — the capability ran successfully against the synthetic dataset, with a named artifact ID, chart, or log entry behind it.
  • Design-complete — specified and implemented in code, but not yet exercised against a named run.
  • [Projected] / [Benchmarked] — forward-looking targets, or comparisons drawn from named external industry figures; never presented as something the system has already achieved.

Nothing in Maldros is production-deployed, and where I state a design target rather than a measured result I say so in the same sentence — because at the level this system is meant to be evaluated, a claim that reads well until someone traces it to source is worse than no claim at all. This is a single-operator simulation, run through script execution against a synthetic but analytically rich dataset that models fraud, abuse, and financial-impact analytics at an AI company. There is no live operator interface yet — an approved design mockup exists, but it is not wired to data — and I name no specific prior employer or job description as the origin of this system. The final two topics are given over entirely to what is and is not built, and to the system’s known limitations, because honest scope is part of the engineering here, not a hedge against it.

Executive Summary · L1

Maldros ran a full analytics investigation — from a raw business question to an executive briefing — autonomously in 288.9 seconds, and the governance held the whole way: the L1 gate blocked that first run's own draft, blocked 14 of 18 Storyteller runs across Phase 1 development, and released a report only once every claim traced to a source — with a human sign-off gate that never auto-approved.

The speed is the least interesting part. The differentiator is that it cost nothing in accountability — and that one property, governance enforced mechanically as hard rules the language model cannot talk its way past, is the thread this case study returns to at every layer. Everything here is validated via simulation against a synthetic dataset; nothing is production-deployed.

Topic 01 · The problem the system solves Validated via simulation
Finding

A governed nine-agent system ran a full analytics investigation in 288.9 seconds — and the abuse it surfaced was invisible to every aggregate view.

A single analytics engineer cannot, by hand, hold a semantic layer consistent, keep pipelines healthy, review experiments with real statistical rigor, and turn all of it into stakeholder-ready reporting at the rate a fast-moving AI company throws off new questions. Maldros was my test of whether a governed, multi-agent system could close that gap. Its first validated demonstration ran the complete cycle — hypothesis, data analysis, statistical validation, and stakeholder narrative — autonomously in 288.9 seconds, against a task the implementation plan estimates at two to five analyst-days, and it did so without bypassing the audit trail or the governance gates that are what make the result trustworthy in the first place.

Impact

The speed is the least interesting part. What matters is that it cost nothing in auditability, citation discipline, or human sign-off authority — which turns "hire more analysts" from an obvious answer into a false binary, where the alternative is to build the leverage layer once and let scarce human judgment concentrate on the irreducible 20% that actually needs it.

The finding itself is the kind aggregate monitoring structurally misses. The population-level Q1 abuse rate was not elevated at all — it sat at 0.946× the non-Q1 average, slightly below normal. The real signal was concentration: a 41-account coordinated cluster operating at 16.54× the baseline rate, carrying $5.89M in Q1 financial impact that no dashboard watching the aggregate would ever surface. That is the underlying problem class Maldros exists to exercise — real findings can be structurally non-obvious, and a system that only ever looks at aggregates will systematically miss them.

Why this scales beyond one question

The load-bearing design decision was to treat "the analytics engineer's job" as nine narrow-mandate agents rather than one large model doing everything — because narrow mandates produce auditable failures; monolithic agents produce inscrutable ones. Each agent gets a bounded toolset and a typed, provenance-stamped artifact as its only interface to the rest of the system.

Concentration, not volume: 41 accounts drove Q1 abuse at 16.54× baseline while the population rate sat at 0.946×.

For a hiring manager: treat the 288.9-second runtime as the least important fact on this page, and the governance-intact result — 94.6% citation coverage on the released report, three L1 vetoes passed, no auto-approval — as the one that actually separates this build from a faster, less careful alternative.

Topic 02 · The target users and use cases Validated via simulation
Finding

Maldros has exactly one operator and one class of beneficiary — and that single-operator design is load-bearing, not a shortcut.

Maldros has one direct user — a single analytics engineer, in this build me, working through a six-dashboard console — and a second, indirect class of beneficiary: the non-technical stakeholders who receive the plain-language briefings it produces. That structure is deliberate. The operator configures and governs the system; stakeholders consume its outputs without needing to understand the mechanics. It is a direct reflection of the mandate the system is built against — one analytics engineer making a small data team operate at roughly ten times its unaided size — and it is a use-case design, not a limitation of the build.

Impact

A system built for many simultaneous operators would look materially different: role-based access controls, concurrent session management, shared audit trails, multi-user governance surfaces. Maldros has none of those — not by oversight, but because the single-operator constraint was load-bearing from the first specification decision. It bought a leaner, more auditable system: every action attributable to one principal, every governance decision owned by one person, and the Confirmation Gate's no-auto-approve rule enforceable without having to adjudicate competing approvals.

Naming the users precisely is itself the point. A system that claims to serve "analytics teams" broadly while having one operator and one domain overstates its reach; one that names its single operator and its handful of validated use cases makes a claim a reviewer can check against the artifact trail. The absence of multi-user machinery is an engineering choice with a documented rationale in the project's own out-of-scope notes — what honest scope looks like in a real project rather than a demo.

Two users, two interface layers, two quality guarantees

The operator and the beneficiary are treated as distinct interfaces rather than collapsed into one. The governance layer governs the operator's interface; the Storyteller Agent's deterministic veto rules govern the stakeholder's. The beneficiary never logs in or configures a query — their "interface" is a read-only, self-contained Mode B briefing that opens with the finding, states the financial stakes, and closes with a plain-language recommendation.

Recommendation

The system routes findings to the right people; building trust with those people stays a human job, and the case study says so rather than papering over it.

For a hiring manager: treat the single-operator scope as a deliberate, documented design choice with a stated multi-operator extension path — the Confirmation Gate, Review Queue, and notification layer are all multi-operator-capable in design — not as a ceiling the architecture cannot cross.

Topic 03 · Business value and outcomes delivered Validated via simulation
Finding

Across six validated phases, the system delivered analyst-quality work at machine speed — with governance intact, not traded away to get there.

Across six validated simulation phases, Maldros demonstrated the proposition the whole system exists to prove: autonomous, multi-agent analytical work that meets a professional quality bar — an evidenced finding, full provenance, stakeholder-ready output — at a fraction of the time a human analyst would need, and without bypassing the governance controls that make the results trustworthy. Every outcome that follows is validated via simulation against a synthetic but analytically rich dataset. None of it is a production result, and none of it is presented as one.

Impact

The significance is not the speed, real as it is. It is that the speed was never traded against governance: the first pipeline run's own draft was blocked by the L1 gate, and the report eventually released had 94.6% of its factual claims traced to a source, all three deterministic L1 vetoes passed, and no auto-approval at the Confirmation Gate. A system that produces fast output by quietly cutting corners on auditability is not a leverage multiplier — it is a liability with a short time-to-incident. These outcomes demonstrate leverage and auditability together, because that specific combination is what makes an autonomous analytical system viable in a business rather than merely impressive in a demo.

Why phase-level outcomes, not one composite number

Reporting by phase rather than as a single aggregate multiplier was a deliberate credibility decision. A composite "so many times better" claim is neither falsifiable nor believable to a technical reviewer; a phase-level outcome is, because each one carries a specific artifact ID, a specific passing criterion, and a specific result. Where a target set in the architecture spec was not met, I name it rather than let an aggregate absorb it — the same standard the system enforces on its own reports, turned on my own case study.

Topic 04 · Technical architecture and system design Validated via simulation
Finding

Governance is enforced in the architecture, not by convention — a deterministic bottom layer holds a veto the language model cannot override.

Maldros is not a model sitting behind a query box. It is a seven-layer architecture whose layers communicate only through typed, provenance-stamped, immutable artifacts — hand-off records written once, fingerprinted with a content hash, and never edited in place — and whose lowest layer, a set of plain deterministic rules with no language model involved, holds a veto that nothing above it, including the LLM orchestrator, is allowed to override. The single choice that organizes everything else is that governance is enforced structurally rather than by convention: the Storyteller Agent cannot ship a report with missing citations, not because a human catches the gap, but because the report is blocked at the artifact level before it can leave the pipeline.

Impact

Structural governance versus convention is the difference between a system that degrades gracefully as operator attention wanes and one that degrades silently. In a convention-governed system, quality depends on a human remembering to check the right things; when attention lapses, the checks lapse with it and nobody notices. In Maldros the deterministic bottom layer runs those checks automatically, and the agent requesting the output cannot switch them off.

That shows up in three concrete places. The Phase 1 report's 94.6% citation coverage was not a number a reviewer signed off on afterward — it was what survived a deterministic citation-coverage veto that blocked 14 of 18 Storyteller runs during development. The Phase 6 interception of the system's own self-improvement proposal was automatic; the Confirmation Gate cannot be talked past by the agent that made the proposal, however high its confidence. And the twelve permanently-locked Design Invariants are constraints the system cannot reason its way out of. The judgment to take from this is that I made the system structurally incapable of certain failure modes rather than layering procedural checks that only catch failures once they have already happened.

Evidence

7

Inference stack · L1 vetoes L5
5

Each of those structural choices answers a specific failure mode a conventional LLM-wrapper design leaves open: silent schema-contract failures (the L1 veto), unreproducible findings (the immutable, content-hashed artifact store), a language model's narrative overriding a correct data signal (the inference stack's arbitration rule), inscrutable monolithic failures (the narrow-mandate agent roster), and self-improvement plateaus (the Algorithmic Rule's mandatory exploration budget).

Seven layers, each crossed only by a typed, immutable artifact
  • Layer 1 · Data Ingestion — synthetic-dataset generation, Parquet export, DuckDB ingest in simulation (BigQuery in production), external-intelligence retrieval.
  • Layer 2A · Knowledge — the Obsidian vault (the Second Brain), sentence-transformer embeddings, a local vector index, the Constraint Register.
  • Layer 2B · Data — DuckDB over Parquet in simulation (BigQuery with dbt model layers in production); schema contracts enforced by dbt tests.
  • Layer 3 · Agent Execution — the nine agents, exchanging typed artifacts that are immutable once emitted.
  • Layer 4 · Self-Improving Cycle — telemetry capture, the Promotion Gate, the Few-Shot Bank, and the Algorithmic Rule (a hard-coded 10% exploration budget).
  • Layer 5 · Invention & Reporting — the Forge (seven reasoning modes), Red-Team stress-testing, the Discovery Report standard, and AIMS routing.
  • Layer 6 · Self-Improvement — the recursive-improvement loop: bottleneck detection, sandbox testing, staged rollout behind a portability wrapper.
  • Layer 7 · Governance — the twelve Design Invariants, the Confirmation Gate (no auto-approve), the approval ladder, and the full audit trail.

Every hand-off conforms to one fixed envelope — a typed record carrying an artifact ID, a schema version, the producing agent, a provenance list of upstream artifact IDs, a content hash, a confidence score, and a known-limitations field. The Diagnostic Agent validates every envelope on receipt: a missing required field is an L2 failure, and a wrong producing_agent for the hand-off position is an L3 contract violation — both halt the pipeline rather than warn. Immutability is what makes the trail trustworthy: a correction produces a new versioned artifact referencing the original, so the complete chain from question to stakeholder output can be reconstructed, every intermediate step and correction included.

The data layer is the one deliberate, named substitution: DuckDB reading Parquet stands in for the production target of BigQuery with dbt Core and its Semantic Layer. The migration is a component swap at Layer 2B — everything above it (the agent architecture, the artifact schemas, the governance model, the Second Brain) stays unchanged. I name the gap plainly: the full natural-language → dbt Semantic Layer → BigQuery-SQL path is design-complete, not validated via simulation, so every query-time claim here is a claim about DuckDB over Parquet and is labeled that way.

Governance sits at Layer 7 with veto authority; agent execution at Layer 3 is where the work happens — the two the diagram makes focal.
Static seven-layer architecture diagram, built to the visual design system, with the simulation-versus-production substitution shown as callouts. Alongside it, an interactive map of the eight-agent investigation chain steps through the eleven-step lifecycle — built in a later sub-pass with a static fallback, illustrating how the process works, never a live running system.
Figure 4. A new visualization built for the case study — not a screenshot of running software.

Risks, named rather than smoothed over. Five stand out. Claude Code's sequential execution is a throughput ceiling at Phase 4 and beyond, mitigated by design — the portability wrapper puts every model call behind one interface so the agent layer can swap to another orchestration environment without a rebuild. The DuckDB/Parquet substitution is a genuine simulation-versus-production gap. The single-operator build leaves multi-tenant behavior unverified — no role-based access control, no concurrent-operator review. The immutable artifact store grows without bound (the Phase 6 run alone produced 175 artifacts) and still needs a retention policy. And L1 veto rules must be calibrated precisely, or their determinism turns into false halts — the veto rules were calibrated through iterative testing — 14 of 18 Phase 1 development runs were blocked before one cleared all three — not through analytical derivation. The standing tradeoff is governance rigidity against raw throughput: every significant output requires a human sign-off, and Design Invariant #4 hard-limits the output rate to human review capacity. I accept that explicitly — generating proposals faster than a human can review them would defeat the point of the gate.

Recommendation

For an engineering leader: focus not on the 288.9-second Phase 1 result but on the governance architecture that produced it intact — the L1 citation veto that blocked 14 of 18 Storyteller runs during Phase 1 development, the Confirmation Gate that held a self-generated proposal without approving it, and the Algorithmic Rule that keeps the self-improvement cycle from plateauing. These are the structural properties that make a fast pipeline safe to run without someone watching it continuously.

For a technical reviewer: read the artifact envelope, the content-hashed immutability rule, and the L0–L4 Diagnostic escalation ladder as one mechanism — an append-only, reconstructable audit trail — and check that every capability claim in this document is labeled validated-via-simulation or design-complete accordingly.

Topic 05 · Implementation approach and development methodology Validated via simulation
Finding

The build discipline is the first deliverable, not the last check.

Maldros was engineered with a methodology that treats its own construction as a governance artifact rather than as project-management overhead layered on afterward. Every decision is traceable through a mandatory, append-only change log; every specification source is arranged in an explicit authority hierarchy so conflicts resolve deterministically rather than by per-session judgment; every session transition produces a complete handoff a future session can reconstruct from without loss; and every phase transition is blocked until the prior phase's exit criteria are confirmed rather than assumed. That discipline is what makes a six-phase autonomous system maintainable across dozens of sessions by a single operator — and it is part of the engineering, not paperwork wrapped around it.

Impact

The reason it matters is auditability. When a technical evaluator asks how they can know the system does what I say it does, the answer is not "trust me" or "run it and see." It is that every specification line in the three source documents carries an explicit operator directive requiring it to be implemented in full; that every decision has a change-log entry; that every phase transition has confirmed exit criteria; and that every session produces a documented handoff. That makes the claim auditable rather than merely plausible.

The methodology exists to solve a failure mode created by the build's own constraints — a single operator, across dozens of finite-context sessions, with no state carried between them except what is explicitly written to files. The implementation plan names the risk in as many words: "The primary risk is not token limits or session limits. The primary risk is architectural drift caused by inadequate context preservation." The answer is to make the continuity layer — not the code — the primary artifact each session reads first and writes last.

The design rests on four decisions: a three-document specification hierarchy with deterministic precedence; an operator-directive framework of six standing rules that govern every development decision; the three-file continuity layer itself (decisions and framing, phase-and-KPI progression, and a change log of every modification); and a phase-gated build in which a standing directive requires an explicit gap-audit against the prior phase's exit criteria before any new phase begins. Those decisions are enforced through five concrete mechanisms — a session-start protocol that makes the continuity records the sole mandatory read; a change-log convention requiring every modification to produce a summarized, dated entry; a starter-message protocol that ends every session with a paste-ready handoff block; a context-window monitoring rule with three mandatory checkpoints; and a file-write verification rule that reads back the tail of every file after writing it.

The methodology corrects its own gaps — the P-020 rule was born from a real failure

The file-write verification rule is not theoretical. In two consecutive sessions, two topics were drafted and apparently appended, the continuity records were updated to record both complete, and a silent truncation went undetected until a later session read the actual file and found only a partial stub. That failure produced the read-back rule (P-020), published here as part of the methodology rather than hidden — a living governance layer that corrects its own gaps, not a plan written once and never revisited.

The three-file continuity layer is the persistent state; each session reads it first and writes it last, with the gap-audit as the one gated checkpoint.
Static continuity-lifecycle schematic: the continuity files in forest (authority and stability), the gap-audit checkpoint in amber (the single focal governance step), and a callout — a session is continuity-complete only when all three files are updated and a starter message is produced.
Figure 5. The continuity layer as primary artifact. A diagram of the build process — not a screenshot of running software.

The methodology is also honest about time. The implementation plan states the scope verbatim: "A genuinely working Phase 1 demonstration … is achievable in two to four weeks of focused work. A production-quality Phase 4 system … is three to six months of serious engineering. The full seven-phase architecture as specified is a six- to twelve-month build." A methodology that sets accurate expectations is more credible than one that promises faster delivery.

Recommendation

For a technical evaluator: read this methodology the way you would read a system's governance architecture — as a signal of how the engineer thinks about failure modes, not just success cases. The session protocol, the phase-gate gap-audit, and the three-file continuity layer are the same kind of structural enforcement Maldros applies to its own analytical outputs.

For a business stakeholder: read the continuity layer as what converts a single-operator build into a system that does not depend on one person's memory — anyone who can read the project's continuity records can reconstruct exactly where the build stands, what has been decided, and what comes next.

Topic 06 · Agent architecture, responsibilities, and interactions Validated via simulation
Finding

Narrow mandates produce auditable failures; monolithic agents produce inscrutable ones.

A single analytical agent that investigates, validates, and communicates in one inference pass cannot be audited when it fails — there is no structural way to identify which of its capabilities produced the wrong output. Maldros decomposes the analytical lifecycle into nine agents — Orchestrator, Data Architect, Analyst, Statistician, Storyteller, Diagnostic, Healing, and Red-Team, which together compose the investigation chain, plus the Forge, the Phase 5 invention agent that sits outside it — each with a bounded mandate (what it is responsible for) and a bounded toolset (what it is allowed to do). The two are designed as a pair, not chosen independently: a narrow mandate without a bounded toolset still permits cross-component corruption, and a bounded toolset without a clear mandate still permits authority creep — so the pairing itself, mandate and tools specified together, is the unit of governance. When any component fails, the failure propagates through the typed artifact envelope, is caught by the Diagnostic Agent's assertion layer, and is attributable to a specific bounded component at a specific hand-off step. This is governance by design, not governance by policy.

Impact

That pairing is the prerequisite for the system's twelve Design Invariants being enforceable rather than aspirational. An invariant a sufficiently capable monolithic component can circumvent is not an invariant — it is a guideline. Each agent's toolset boundary is therefore a structural enforcement mechanism rather than a rule someone has to remember to check: the Diagnostic Agent cannot corrupt the state it monitors because it holds no write access anywhere; the Red-Team Agent cannot affect the production system it stress-tests because it has no production access at all; the Storyteller Agent cannot introduce an analytical error because it performs no derivation.

The core problem the decomposition solves is attributability. When an analytical system produces a finding that is wrong, inconsistent, or non-compliant, someone has to be able to say exactly where the failure occurred, what produced it, and which constraint it violated. In a monolithic system that question has no structural answer; in Maldros it does. The typed artifact envelope records the producing agent, the phase of origin, the provenance chain, and the known limitations declared at the moment of production — and the Diagnostic Agent validates every envelope the instant it is received: a malformed envelope is a typed failure (severity L2), a producing-agent mismatch is a contract violation (L3), and a Design Invariant violation is an immediate halt (L4). Failure is made legible before it ever reaches the analyst.

Five design decisions produced that architecture, and each is a choice I can defend rather than a default I inherited. First, each agent's mandate and toolset were specified together, not independently — an agent that can only do what its mandate requires cannot overreach — derived from the governance requirement that every failure be attributable to a specific bounded component. Second, the Diagnostic Agent is permanently read-only: a monitoring agent with write access could corrupt the very state it measures, and its integrity would then require a second monitor watching the first — an infinite regress a read-only constraint simply terminates. Third, the Capability Bundle — a snapshot of the Cross-Domain Intelligence Layer for the current task context — is the first artifact emitted on every task, before any downstream agent begins, with capabilities evaluated-but-not-met logged explicitly rather than silently dropped, so a task whose lineage trace lacks a Capability Bundle is itself a Diagnostic L3 failure. Fourth, the Storyteller Agent is pure output transformation: it renders validated findings into a technical layer and a plain-language layer but never derives a finding or re-validates an inference, and three deterministic L1 vetoes run before any report ships. Fifth, the Red-Team Agent's adversarial pass is kept structurally independent: it runs after the Statistician's validation and before the Storyteller, and stress-tests the Analyst's proposed detection approach on that methodology's own structural merits, so a high confidence score from validation cannot anchor the adversarial assessment and quietly soften it.

The nine agents divide the work as follows, each described by its mandate, its bounded toolset, and its current maturity. The first eight compose the investigation chain; the ninth, the Forge, runs Phase 5 invention cycles outside it.

The Orchestrator decomposes each task, routes sub-tasks to the specialist agents, queries the Second Brain before every task, and emits the Capability Bundle as the first artifact on every task — and it produces no analytical findings of its own. Its toolset is Second Brain query (vector and keyword search), artifact read, task routing, and Capability Bundle emission; an Orchestrator output missing a Capability Bundle in its lineage trace is a Diagnostic L3 failure. Maturity: design-complete, with Capability Bundle emission validated via simulation in Phase 6.

The Data Architect Agent designs, generates, and validates data models and semantic-layer definitions. Its toolset is schema query (read-only), generation of data-model and semantic-layer definitions written to draft only — never merged to production — dbt test execution, and artifact write; every proposed model requires human one-click approval before it can execute. The agent proposes; a human authorizes. Maturity: design-complete.

The Analyst Agent runs the end-to-end investigation: hypothesis formation, data query through the semantic-layer interface, Python execution (pandas, polars, networkx, scipy), interpretation, and recommendations. Its toolset adds Second Brain write access and web search. SQL is available only in a sandboxed mode and is never its primary interface — the default path is natural language to execution plan to result. Its one named limitation is carried in the open: the current DuckDB-over-Parquet query implementation is built around the Phase 1 investigation and is not yet generalized to arbitrary free-text questions. Maturity: validated via simulation — the Phase 1 investigation ran end-to-end in 288.9 seconds.

The Statistician Agent validates every inference the Analyst produces and runs experiment analysis — sample-ratio-mismatch (SRM) detection, novelty-effect checks, power analysis — and issues ship / no-ship verdicts on A/B tests. Its toolset is Python execution (statsmodels, scipy, pingouin), artifact read/write, Second Brain write, and data query for statistical validation only. Every confidence interval, p-value, and effect size in any downstream artifact must trace back to a Statistician artifact in the provenance chain. Maturity: validated via simulation in Phase 1 and Phase 3.

The Storyteller Agent produces the dual-layer output — a technical layer for engineers and data scientists, a plain-language layer for product and business stakeholders — and it translates without deriving. It fully renders its own charts (matplotlib/networkx to PNG); specifying a chart without rendering it is treated as a system failure. Its toolset is artifact read (all types), chart rendering, and artifact write (the Discovery Report and the AIMS Mode B briefing). Three deterministic L1 vetoes run before a report can ship, and all three must pass: a causal-language veto (no causal assertion without causal evidence upstream — a correlation dressed as causation is blocked), a citation-coverage veto (every factual claim must link to the citation index, or the report is blocked), and an omission-audit veto (every finding flagged as material must appear, or the report is blocked). Maturity: validated via simulation — in Phase 1 the compliant report reached 94.6% citation coverage, 88 of 93 claims; 14 of 18 runs were blocked by this three-veto gate over the course of development.

The Diagnostic Agent performs continuous, read-only monitoring of pipeline health, schema contracts, output drift, and data quality. Its toolset is artifact read (all types), metadata query, and dbt test-result read — and no write access to any system, which is precisely the property that makes it trustworthy as the assertion layer. It escalates along a five-level ladder with numeric thresholds (PSI is the Population Stability Index, a standard measure of how far a distribution has drifted from its baseline):

  • L0 · Nominal — all assertions passing, PSI below 0.10, latency under 2× the rolling median → log only.
  • L1 · Self-heal — a single recognized assertion failure, or PSI 0.10–0.20 → hand to the Healing Agent, notify the Orchestrator.
  • L2 · Elevated — an assertion-failure rate above 2% in a 60-minute window, or PSI 0.20–0.50, or latency above 3× the rolling median, or a Healing retry count of 2 → hand to Healing, pause new work on the affected pipeline, open AIMS Mode A.
  • L3 · Human escalation — an unrecognized failure class, a Healing retry count of 3 or more without resolution, an assertion-failure rate above 5% in a 15-minute window, a safety-class assertion failure, or a cascade spanning two or more agents → move the pipeline to supervised mode, open AIMS Mode B.
  • L4 · Halt — a Design Invariant violation, an audit-trail corruption risk, or PSI above 0.50 → immediate halt, immediate human page, no autonomous action until a human clears it.

Maturity: validated via simulation — in Phase 2, all three injected failure classes were detected at the correct severity and escalated correctly.

The Healing Agent performs cross-domain repair: it characterizes a failure, retrieves candidate repair strategies from five analogue domains (Medicine, Materials Science, Systems Biology, Military Logistics, and Law), scores them, applies one, and verifies the result against the Diagnostic Agent's assertions. Its toolset is CDI Layer read, Python execution for remediation scripts, artifact write (the healing record), and table read — and it produces draft pull requests only, never a production merge. It escalates to a human only when all six maximum-capacity conditions hold at once:

  • Strategy exhaustion — every applicable repair strategy has been attempted or ruled out with a documented precondition mismatch.
  • Retry exhaustion — the Healing retry count has reached 3 or more.
  • Synthesis exhaustion — composite strategies have been attempted.
  • Budget exhaustion — the per-failure compute and time budget is consumed.
  • No-progress condition — the last several attempts produced no measurable improvement in the Diagnostic assertions.
  • Root reached or unreachable — the minimum causal chain has been computed, and remediation at the root either failed or lies outside the system's authority.

Maturity: validated via simulation — in Phase 2 all three injected failure classes (structural break, gradual degradation, cascade) were autonomously remediated, and human escalation was never triggered because the six-condition threshold was never reached.

The Red-Team Agent stress-tests every output adversarially before it can reach the analyst, running twelve evasion categories against each proposed metric, methodology, data product, or experiment framework in a sandbox and returning one of three verdicts: Robust (no breakthrough even under a maximum-intelligence adversary), Conditionally Robust (a breakthrough only under named, low-probability conditions), or Brittle (a feasible breakdown exists at acceptable stakeholder effort). A Brittle verdict blocks the output from the analyst queue absent explicit escalation and human review. Its toolset is artifact read (the artifact under test), Python execution for attack simulation in the sandbox, and artifact write (the Red-Team report) — with no access to live data and none to any production system. The twelve evasion categories are:

  • E1 · Feature manipulation — manipulating the input features a detector relies on in order to evade it.
  • E2 · Temporal evasion — exploiting gaps between measurement time-windows to move activity through unobserved.
  • E3 · Threshold gaming — keeping activity just below the thresholds that would trigger detection.
  • E4 · Coordinated mimicry — a coordinated cluster imitating the behavior patterns of legitimate accounts to blend in.
  • E5 · Signal dilution — spreading the abuse signal thinly across many accounts or across time.
  • E6 · Adversarial labeling — poisoning the labels or feedback the detection model learns from.
  • E7 · Concept-drift exploitation — exploiting periods when the model's learned patterns have drifted out of date.
  • E8 · Sampling bias — exploiting gaps and blind spots in how the data covers the population.
  • E9 · Proxy substitution — substituting proxy signals that bypass the specific measure a detector keys on.
  • E10 · Model inversion — inferring the model's internals from its outputs and using that to evade it.
  • E11 · Infrastructure blind spots — exploiting pipeline gaps: missing tables, NULL handling, and similar seams.
  • E12 · Governance-gap exploitation — exploiting review-queue delays or policy gaps in the governance layer.

Maturity: validated via simulation — in Phase 3, three experiments were analyzed blind and correct verdicts produced on all three without advance knowledge of which pathology each carried; in Phase 5, the "Spectral Coordination Sieve" novel detection framework was stress-tested and returned Conditionally Robust.

The Forge Agent is the invention engine added in Phase 5, and it is the one agent that sits outside the investigation chain: rather than analyzing the data, it generates new analytical frameworks, measurement approaches, and data-product architectures from first principles. Every output must declare which of the seven reasoning modes produced it before its content can be read — a governance mechanism under Design Invariant 7, on the reasoning that mode confusion is the dominant failure mode in analytical AI. The Innovation Mandate (Design Invariant 12) requires that at least 15% of first-principles invention cycles produce genuinely novel output rather than incremental refinement, and anything incremental must be labeled as such explicitly. Its pipeline ordering is deliberately inverted relative to the investigation chain — the Red-Team stress test runs before statistical validation, so a proposed framework must survive an adversary before it earns the cost of being measured. All thirteen Invention Pipeline Report assets are emitted on every cycle regardless of whether the Pre-Screen Gate passes, so a rejected invention leaves the same audit trail as an accepted one. Maturity: validated via simulation — the Phase 5 run produced the "Spectral Coordination Sieve," a novel detection framework generated with no prior template, which returned a Conditionally Robust Red-Team verdict.

The toolset boundary is the enforcement mechanism — the architecture is what makes the governance hold

Four interaction patterns compose these agents into a pipeline. The Orchestrator fans out to every downstream agent through the Capability Bundle, making the capability state at task initiation part of the auditable record. The Analyst, Statistician, and Red-Team form a sequential validation chain — the Analyst's Evidence Bundle feeds the Statistician, whose Statistical Result feeds the Red-Team, whose verdict and report feed the Storyteller, which consumes all three together — with each hand-off a typed, immutable artifact, so an agent that receives artifacts out of sequence trips a Diagnostic L3 failure. The Diagnostic and Healing Agents run as a continuously operating parallel loop, watching every hand-off and re-running assertions against the repaired state without interrupting the pipeline unless severity reaches L3 or L4. And the Red-Team is the final gate before stakeholder delivery: no output reaches the Storyteller — and therefore no stakeholder — without a Red-Team verdict.

Eight bounded agents, four interaction patterns: a typed-artifact chain the Diagnostic loop watches end to end, with the Red-Team as the final gate before any stakeholder sees an output.
Interactive agent-interaction map: the sequential Analyst → Statistician → Red-Team → Storyteller chain in forest, the Red-Team gate as the single amber focal element, the parallel Diagnostic/Healing loop as a monitoring overlay. The measurable outcomes, all validated via simulation, show the architecture doing what it was designed to do. In Phase 1, the released report cleared all three L1 vetoes at 94.6% citation coverage (88 of 93 claims), and 14 of 18 Storyteller runs were blocked during development before one did — a system that blocks non-compliant reports mechanically has a categorically different governance posture from one that would have shipped them before a human noticed. In Phase 2, the Diagnostic and Healing Agents detected all three injected failure classes at the correct severity, classified each by failure type, and autonomously remediated all three using cross-domain repair strategies, with no human escalation. In Phase 3, the Red-Team analyzed three experiments blind and produced correct verdicts on all three: NO_SHIP (sample ratio mismatch detected), HOLD_FOR_HARDENING (a Brittle finding plus a novelty effect), and SHIP at Conditionally Robust. In Phase 5, the "Spectral Coordination Sieve" was submitted without pre-validation and returned Conditionally Robust. And in Phase 6, the full investigation pipeline audited 175 real artifacts with 100% correct Mode A / Mode B routing (an 89 / 86 split, zero misrouted), ran without human scaffolding at any intermediate step, and reached exactly one human-involvement point — the Confirmation Gate intercepting a self-generated improvement proposal and queuing it for sign-off with no auto-approve, functioning precisely as designed.

Three risks and one standing tradeoff are worth naming rather than smoothing over. The Analyst Agent's generalization is incomplete — the current query implementation is shaped around the Phase 1 investigation and does not yet handle arbitrary free-text questions — carried openly here and in the build-status and known-limitations sections, with a generalized query interface flagged as a natural Phase 7+ item. The Red-Team Agent's calibration needs periodic validation: an agent that always returns Robust has converged to a local minimum and is not working hard enough, which is why the Phase 3 exit criterion required it to find an injected Brittle design with no advance notice — the correct calibration signal is the proportion of injected flaws it catches, not the proportion of Robust verdicts it issues. And the single-operator sequential execution model constrains throughput at Phase 4 and beyond — documented, not hidden — with a clean migration path already in place: the LLM abstraction wrapper, the typed artifact envelope, and the CDI Layer interfaces let the agent layer swap to a parallel-execution substrate without a rebuild. The standing tradeoff is nine agents versus fewer, more capable ones: fewer would be simpler to operate but harder to audit, and the nine-agent decomposition deliberately trades operational simplicity for governance precision.

Recommendation

For a technical evaluator: test this architecture with a single question — if the Analyst Agent produced a wrong finding, how would you know, and how long would it take? Here the answer is structural: the Statistician validates every inference in a separate bounded pass, the Red-Team tries to break the finding before it can reach the analyst queue, and the Storyteller's three L1 vetoes block the report if any claim is unattributed, any causal assertion lacks causal evidence, or any material finding is missing. The question is answerable because the architecture makes it answerable — not because a reviewer happened to be paying attention.

For a team weighing adoption: decide which governance properties you need mechanically enforced and which you are willing to leave to process compliance. The bounded-mandate / bounded-toolset architecture delivers the former. It does not make the system infallible — the Analyst's generalization gap and the sequential-execution bottleneck are real and documented — but it does make the system auditable: when something is wrong, it can be found, attributed, and corrected without reconstructing what a monolithic agent was "thinking."

Topic 07 · Workflow orchestration and end-to-end automation Validated via simulation
Finding

Every investigation is at once a finding and the complete audit trail of how it was reached.

A natural-language question enters the pipeline at Step 1 and a governed, auditable stakeholder output exits at Step 10 — and because every intermediate hand-off is materialized as a typed, immutable artifact, each investigation is simultaneously a conclusion and a full record of how that conclusion was produced. This is the eleven-step execution lifecycle, and it is the architecture's integration test: not the claim that Maldros coordinates nine agents, but the claim that the coordination itself produces a verifiable record of how a conclusion was reached, not merely what was concluded. Every step emits a typed artifact. No step can be skipped. No agent receives input it did not read from the prior artifact. The governance properties of the output — that every claim is attributed, every inference validated, and an adversary tried and failed to break the finding before it shipped — are not policy applied after the fact. They are structural consequences of the way the workflow is wired.

Impact

Analytics workflows fail in two different ways, and most process fixes address only one. In the first, a finding is produced but never validated, which manufactures false confidence. In the second, a finding is validated but the validation record is not preserved, which produces conclusions no one can defend once they are questioned. Maldros closes both at once: the inference-validation stage (the Statistician, Step 7) and the adversarial stress test (the Red-Team, Step 8) are not diligence a careful analyst might optionally perform — they are mandatory pipeline stages the Storyteller cannot bypass, because the Storyteller has no valid input from which to produce an output until the Red-Team report exists to consume. The governance is enforced by the dependency structure of the pipeline, not by the good intentions of whoever is reviewing the result.

The business consequence is that a finding produced by this workflow is defeasible in the precise sense: if it later proves wrong, the audit trail shows exactly where the failure entered — which agent, which step, which artifact — and the correction can be applied at that point and propagated forward. In a manual workflow, "we checked the numbers" is a statement about intent; in Maldros it is a statement about which typed artifact was produced at which step by which agent, traceable to the specific inputs it consumed.

The one job of the orchestration layer is narrow and worth stating exactly: ensure that a natural-language question, submitted by a human analyst, produces a governed stakeholder output with a complete, traceable execution record — without requiring that analyst to sequence, coordinate, or hand off work between agents by hand. The Orchestrator handles sequencing; each agent handles its bounded function; the artifact store preserves every intermediate output; the routing layer classifies the final output for its delivery channel. The analyst's only required touchpoints are the question at Step 1 and the governance gate at Step 10; everything between runs autonomously. This addresses not a shortage of careful analysts but a structural reliability defect that adding careful people does not fix: under deadline pressure validation steps get skipped, when they are skipped there is no record of what was and was not checked, and even a rigorously executed manual workflow does not compound — each investigation starts cold, with prior findings and known failure modes living in individual analysts' memory.

Five design decisions produced this workflow. First, the typed artifact hand-off is the primary design constraint, not an implementation detail: every hand-off is a content-hashed, immutable JSON artifact carrying a fixed envelope — identifier, type, producing agent, timestamp, provenance chain, schema version, content, declared known-limitations, and confidence score — and the Diagnostic Agent validates every envelope on receipt, so a missing field is a typed failure (L2) and the wrong producing agent for a position is a contract violation (L3). This is what makes partial execution impossible. Second, sequential execution is a deliberate constraint, not a limitation I failed to remove: the simulation runs a single-operator sequential model in which each step completes before the next begins, which eliminates race conditions and makes artifact ordering deterministic, with the LLM abstraction wrapper, the typed artifact envelope, and the CDI Layer interfaces all designed as clean substitution seams for the parallel-execution migration at Phase 4 and beyond. Third, the Red-Team runs before the Storyteller not as a review but as a prerequisite — its report is a required input in the artifact graph — and the Storyteller's three deterministic vetoes then operate on top of it. Fourth, output routing is part of the workflow rather than an afterthought: every meaningful output passes a deterministic routing decision, and anything that does not clearly qualify for the operational log routes to the stakeholder-briefing channel by default, so there is no unclassified path. Fifth, the Confirmation Gate intercepts before, not after: it catches at Step 10, before any finding is acted on, and its no-auto-approve rule has no exceptions — not on timeout, not on operator absence, not under any phase of self-improvement.

The eleven-step lifecycle, drawn from the architecture specification's worked example (a Q1 API-abuse investigation), runs as follows:

  • Step 1 · Question received — a human analyst submits a natural-language question: whether a Q1 rise in API-abuse volume is driven by coordinated multi-account behavior, and what the financial exposure is.
  • Step 2 · Orchestrator queries the Second Brain — before any analysis, it retrieves prior investigations, relevant metric definitions, external intelligence, and open Constraint Register entries, emitting a Context Bundle.
  • Step 3 · Orchestrator decomposes the task — the question is split into typed sub-tasks for the Analyst, Statistician, Red-Team, and Storyteller.
  • Step 4 · Diagnostic Agent activates — continuous monitoring of every artifact hand-off begins; monitoring only, no analytical output.
  • Step 5 · Data Architect Agent (conditional) — if the investigation needs data absent from existing mart tables, it generates a model specification with a dbt test suite and submits the draft for human one-click approval; otherwise the step is skipped.
  • Step 6 · Analyst runs the investigation — consuming the Context Bundle and querying through the semantic-layer interface, it selects a reasoning mode (first-principles here, since no high-similarity prior existed), derives graph-theoretic coordination signals, executes in Python (networkx, scipy, pandas), and emits an Evidence Bundle.
  • Step 7 · Statistician validates the inference — it validates the volume spike, the connectivity distribution, the entropy asymmetry, sample-size adequacy, and confounds, flagging limitations explicitly (one trial-tier subgroup, N = 47, was flagged as insufficient), and emits a Statistical Result.
  • Step 8 · Red-Team stress-tests adversarially — running its twelve evasion categories in a sandbox: a signal-dilution attack produced a breakthrough, a data-coverage probe a partial finding, and a coordinated-mimicry test no breakthrough. Verdict: Conditionally Robust, breakthrough conditions named. It emits a Red-Team Report.
  • Step 9 · Storyteller produces the dual-layer output — consuming the Evidence Bundle, Statistical Result, and Red-Team Report together, it checks its three vetoes and, only if all three pass, produces the seven-section Discovery Report and the Mode B briefing.
  • Step 10 · Governance gate — the briefing goes to the analyst, who approves or requests revision; vault entries are written continuously, not gated on approval; any proposed countermeasure routes to the Confirmation Gate, where nothing is auto-approved.
  • Step 11 · Telemetry capture — analyst corrections are captured as telemetry and submitted to the Promotion Gate; generalizable corrections enter the Few-Shot Bank and prime future investigations of similar type.
The same eleven steps, walked one at a time: a question enters at Step 1 and a governed, fully-traceable stakeholder output exits at Step 10, with telemetry captured at Step 11.

Coordination is entirely artifact-mediated — no agent talks to another directly

No agent calls another: the Analyst emits an Evidence Bundle, the Statistician consumes it and emits a Statistical Result, the Red-Team consumes the evidence and the proposed approach and emits its report, and the Storyteller consumes all three and emits the Discovery Report and the Mode B briefing — and any malformed or absent artifact in that chain stops the downstream agent rather than letting it proceed on inferred input. Context retrieval precedes analysis: the Capability Bundle emitted first on every task must carry a recorded CDI Layer query in its lineage, because a Capability Bundle without one is itself a Diagnostic failure. And telemetry closes the loop: a hard-coded 10% exploration budget redirects every tenth investigation cycle to a counter-intuitive hypothesis from the Constraint Register rather than the most similar prior case, keeping the Few-Shot Bank from over-indexing on confirmed approaches.

The routing decision at Step 9 is binary and exhaustive: novel or consequential outputs default to human sign-off; only routine, Robust-verdict work is auto-logged.
Static routing-decision flowchart: the primary decision nodes in forest, the stakeholder-briefing (human-sign-off) outcome as the single amber focal element, the decision-path lines in neutral gray. A novel typology, new metric, new data product, ship/no-ship verdict, or architectural change routes to Mode B; routine heals, exemplar promotions, and Robust-verdict inventions route to Mode A; anything unclear defaults to Mode B.

The measurable outcomes, all validated via simulation, show the workflow doing what it was designed to do. On wall-clock time, the Phase 1 demonstration ran end-to-end in 288.9 seconds and the Phase 6 full-pipeline run in 73.6 seconds, both comfortably under the 30–90-minute architectural target. On analyst time, the design consumes 15–30 minutes per investigation for review and the governance gate while the analytical execution runs automated; measured against a classical equivalent of two to five analyst-days, that is on the order of a 28–80× reduction in analyst-hours — but this is derived from the specification's target figures, not a measurement against a human baseline run in this simulation, and I label it as such. On routing accuracy, the Phase 6 audit put 175 artifacts through the routing logic and produced 100% correct classification (89 Mode A, 86 Mode B), zero misrouted. On governance, the Confirmation Gate intercepted one self-generated improvement proposal and blocked auto-approval exactly as required, and that proposal is currently queued for analyst sign-off. On the output-quality floor, the Storyteller's three vetoes held in Phase 1: 14 of 18 Storyteller runs were blocked by the veto gate during development, and the governed output that cleared it reached 94.6% citation coverage — 88 of 93 claims attributed. And on the self-improvement trajectory, the ten-cycle Phase 4 run showed a one-time edit-distance step reduction across all three tracked query classes when the first exemplar entered the Few-Shot Bank and then a flat line through cycle nine, confirming the telemetry → Promotion Gate → Few-Shot Bank pipeline fires correctly; the larger multi-cycle divergence remains a specified design target illustrated by cross-domain analogy, not a measured result.

Three risks, a substitution, and a standing dependency are worth naming. The sequential-execution model is the binding throughput constraint at Phase 4 and beyond, documented as a known risk, with the migration to a parallel substrate a planned transition that reroutes the artifact store and replaces the LLM abstraction layer without rewriting agent logic. The Mode B throughput ceiling is real: every stakeholder briefing requires human sign-off, and the architecture deliberately throttles self-improvement-proposal generation when the review queue exceeds the analyst's capacity — suspending proposals at the queue's red threshold and, at critical, suspending all generation and triggering a team-expansion signal. The Analyst Agent's generalization gap is carried in the open. The substitution is DuckDB querying Parquet files in place of the intended BigQuery production warehouse — the semantic layer, artifact schemas, and agent logic are deliberately warehouse-agnostic. And the standing dependency is that every artifact write must be immediately followed by a Second Brain vault write; the two are hard-coupled at the code level, evidenced by the Phase 6 run's 100% artifact-to-vault correspondence.

Recommendation

For a technical evaluator: start with the workflow, not the agent roster. The roster names eight capabilities; the eleven-step lifecycle is what shows whether they integrate into something coherent, and the Phase 6 run is the answer — 175 artifacts processed, 100% governed routing, zero human interventions at intermediate steps, one Confirmation Gate intercept behaving exactly as designed. That is an integration-test result, not a feature list.

For an organization weighing adoption: the design question the lifecycle forces is a useful one to ask of any analytics system — which governance properties do we need mechanically enforced, and which are we prepared to maintain through process compliance? From Step 1 through Step 9 the audit trail is a structural output of the workflow, not a documentation obligation. And because the portability wrapper defines the integration contract, adopting the workflow does not require adopting the simulation's specific execution substrate: the execution layer can be replaced while the governance contract is preserved.

Topic 08 · Decision-making frameworks and autonomous capabilities Validated via simulation
Finding

Layer 1 is deterministic — and it can veto the LLM at the top of the stack, whatever the narrative concludes.

Every analytical decision Maldros makes passes through a five-layer inference stack in which Layer 1 — composed entirely of deterministic heuristic rules — can veto the judgment of every layer above it, including the LLM Orchestrator at Layer 5. The LLM does not arbitrate data quality; it cannot override a schema contract; a known-null value in a not-null column is rejected at L1 regardless of what the narrative assessment at the top of the stack concludes. This is a structural property, not a commitment the agents are instructed to honor — correctness-by-construction, not correctness-by-convention. Layered on top of that stack are seven declared reasoning modes, and together the two systems are the decision-making framework: not guidelines agents are asked to follow, but structural constraints that determine what kinds of output the system is able to produce at all.

Impact

This answers the question most often put to any analytical AI: what stops it from hallucinating confidently? The answer here is not prompt engineering, and not agent-level instructions the next API call can contradict — it is an inference hierarchy in which deterministic vetoes at L1 structurally prevent whole classes of output from ever reaching the stakeholder layer, whatever the LLM concludes. The precise way to put it to a technical evaluator is that Maldros is not more constrained than a conventional single-call LLM system; it is differently constrained. Where a single-mode call has no structural limit on what it can assert or how it reached the assertion, this stack makes certain assertions constitutionally unavailable — which is not a ceiling on capability but the mechanism that makes the system's outputs auditable, defensible, and governable as the workload scales.

The framework serves two objectives that pull apart unless the design carries both: every output is produced by a reasoning process appropriate to the question, and every output can be audited — by a human, by the Diagnostic Agent, or by a later session — with a complete record of how it was produced. The five-layer stack delivers the first by constraining how a decision is assembled; the seven-mode declaration rule delivers the second by making the generative process an explicit, load-bearing artifact field rather than a prose afterthought.

Evidence

5
Deterministic (L1) → statistical → physics-based → state-superposition → LLM synthesis (L5). L1's veto cannot be overridden by any higher layer, including the LLM.

7
Analogical, First-Principles, Abductive, Counterfactual, Cross-Domain, Adversarial Game Trees, Bayesian — each declared in every output that invokes it; an artifact with no mode fails L1.
Design Invariants · the operational floor
12
Permanently locked, human-modifiable but system-unmodifiable. Bypassing any is a structural impossibility, not a governance failure.
Exploration budget · hard-coded (Invariant #5)
10%
One in ten cycles redirected to a counter-intuitive hypothesis from the Constraint Register — analyst-adjustable in magnitude, never skippable.

Three failure modes common to analytical AI without structural governance are what the framework exists to prevent. The first is LLM narrative override: absent a deterministic veto, an LLM assessing a dataset can produce a plausible narrative that contradicts what the data contains — most dangerously under data-quality failures or missing provenance — and that narrative reaches the stakeholder; here the L1 checks run before synthesis, a failure at L1 stops the output, and the LLM's competing assessment is never surfaced. The second is mode confusion: most analytical AI calls an LLM once and takes the result, which may have been produced analogically, abductively, or by Bayesian updating with no way to know which — and treating a derivative analogical result as an original first-principles derivation is identified in the architecture as the dominant failure mode; the seven-mode declaration rule is its structural prevention. The third is capability plateau: a self-improving system that only promotes its existing best approaches converges on a local optimum and stops improving, which the hard-coded exploration budget is built to prevent.

Five design decisions produced the framework. L1 is the unconditional veto authority — a hard termination condition, not a weighted input — because a schema-contract violation, a known-bad signature, and a Design-Invariant boundary check are binary conditions, not probabilistic signals to be weighed. Mode declaration is a governance mechanism, not a transparency nicety: a First-Principles output warrants a different validation regime than an Analogical one, so without a declared mode the Diagnostic Agent and the Statistician cannot even select the correct validation logic. The exploration budget is hard-coded as a locked invariant rather than an analyst preference, because a merely encouraged budget gets deprioritized the moment the queue fills. Every agent query runs against the CDI Layer — the continuously-running eight-domain intelligence substrate — before any output, so reasoning is informed by full institutional context rather than the immediate prompt. And twelve permanently-locked Design Invariants sit beneath the whole apparatus as the operational floor, below which the system cannot operate and which no agent, phase, or self-improvement proposal can modify.

The five-layer inference stack processes every question from deterministic to generative, and higher layers cannot override the deterministic vetoes of lower ones:

  • L1 · Heuristic (deterministic; veto authority) — schema-contract validation, known-bad-pattern detection by signature matching, and Design-Invariant boundary checks. An L1 veto propagates straight to the decision output and bypasses every higher layer; these are conditions the LLM never reaches.
  • L2 · Statistical — Bayesian belief networks for data-quality priors, Shannon entropy over distributions, and graph-centrality metrics on entity networks, alongside significance testing. The Phase 1 finding — a 41-account cluster at 16.54× the population rate ratio — was surfaced in part by L2 graph-centrality analysis. Validated via simulation (Phase 1, 288.9s).
  • L3 · Physics-based — power-law distribution fitting (Kolmogorov–Smirnov tested), percolation theory for cluster-growth phase transitions, and entropy-production rate as a data-quality scalar. Design-complete; exercised in the Phase 1 and Phase 2 demonstrations.
  • L4 · State-superposition — Monte Carlo Tree Search over analysis decision trees with Sequential Probability Ratio Testing per branch, pre-staging hypotheses to compress time-to-insight. Design-complete; SPRT demonstrated in Phase 3.
  • L5 · LLM Orchestrator — synthesis and arbitration across the lower layers; proposes actions and produces the final narrative. It is the one layer that cannot override L1 — it synthesizes, it does not overrule. Validated via simulation across all six demonstrated phases.

Seven reasoning modes sit on top of the stack, each declared in every output that invokes it — declaration being a required artifact field, not an annotation:

  • Mode 1 · Analogical (DERIVATIVE) — invoked on a high-similarity prior; the output states the precedent and adaptation rationale, and the Red-Team checks the structural validity of the match. Validated via simulation (Phase 1).
  • Mode 2 · First-Principles — invoked when no high-similarity prior exists; the output carries the full derivation chain. Phase 5 produced the "Spectral Coordination Sieve" under this mode. Validated via simulation (Phase 5).
  • Mode 3 · Abductive — applied to an anomaly with no typology match: what generative process most economically explains this pattern? Validated via simulation (Phase 1).
  • Mode 4 · Counterfactual Simulation — tests whether a proposed metric or rule would have changed a known historical outcome. Phase 3 used it to confirm the SRM correction would not have overturned the NO_SHIP verdict. Validated via simulation (Phase 3).
  • Mode 5 · Cross-Domain Analogy — applied when a solved problem in an adjacent field shares the same underlying structure. The Healing Agent's repair reasoning retrieves across Medicine, Materials Science, Systems Biology, Military Logistics, and Law. Validated via simulation (Phase 2).
  • Mode 6 · Adversarial Game Trees — applied to design where stakeholders optimize against the metric (Stackelberg framing). Phase 3's HOLD_FOR_HARDENING verdict combined a Brittle Red-Team finding with a distinct novelty/Hawthorne effect flagged in validation. Validated via simulation (Phase 3).
  • Mode 7 · Bayesian Updating — applied when signals accumulate slowly. The Phase 4 cycle applies it to the Few-Shot Bank, tripping the Promotion Gate only once the posterior exceeds threshold. Design-complete; exercised in Phase 4.

The Algorithmic Rule — Design Invariant #5 — is hard-coded, not a guideline: the analyst may adjust the percentage in either direction, but the system cannot skip the cycles. The parameter is a 10% mandatory exploration budget: one in ten cycles is redirected to a counter-intuitive, low-probability hypothesis drawn from the open Constraint Register. I have to be precise about the figure attached to it, because it is easy to overstate. The source specification models the per-cycle improvement rate as decaying toward a plateau without the rule and as sustaining compounding with it — but those are illustrative design targets justified by cross-domain analogy, not magnitudes fitted to data, and not yet validated. What the Phase 4 ten-cycle run actually measured was narrower: a one-time edit-distance step reduction (40–53%) across all three tracked query classes when the first exemplar entered the Few-Shot Bank, then a flat line through cycle nine, with the rule firing deterministically on schedule and surfacing a genuinely non-obvious Constraint-Register hypothesis. Maturity: pipeline validated via simulation (Phase 4); the 50-cycle magnitude is an unvalidated design target. The analogues the specification cites for the mechanism are worth naming as its justification: somatic hypermutation in B-cell affinity maturation, AlphaGo Zero's UCB1 exploration bonus in Monte Carlo Tree Search, and Romer endogenous-growth theory's mandatory R&D labor share.

Beneath the stack and the modes sit the twelve permanently-locked Design Invariants — human-modifiable, system-unmodifiable — shown here in full, because the source-citation discipline requires the floor to be shown rather than summarized:

  • 1 · L1 arbitration — deterministic vetoes cannot be overridden by higher inference layers; protects against LLM narrative overriding known-bad data signals.
  • 2 · Explicit human authorization — every consequential action requires it; prevents autonomous deployment of changes affecting production or stakeholders.
  • 3 · Audit-trail completeness — every artifact carries a complete provenance chain; makes findings reproducible and defenses defensible.
  • 4 · Proposal rate ≤ human review capacity — prevents the system generating more changes than the analyst can scrutinize.
  • 5 · The Algorithmic Rule — 10% exploration budget by default, analyst-adjustable either way; prevents over-indexing on known-good paths and plateauing.
  • 6 · Dual-layer output standard — every output has a technical and a plain-language layer; ensures non-technical stakeholders can always understand it.
  • 7 · Generation mode always declared — Analogical vs. First-Principles vs. the extended modes; prevents confusing derivative work for original derivation.
  • 8 · Red-Team sandbox-only, report-only — keeps the adversarial simulation capability from becoming a production risk.
  • 9 · SQL is not the default interface — it is a sandboxed execution capability; enforces natural-language-first, execution-layer-second.
  • 10 · No dark-web or restricted-source data acquisition — a hard safety and compliance boundary.
  • 11 · Strongest frontier model always — the Non-Negotiable Model Foundation; prevents cost-optimization from degrading analytical capability.
  • 12 · Novel inventions a standing priority — the Innovation Mandate; keeps The Forge from drifting toward incremental refinement only.
Mode declaration is a governance mechanism, not a transparency nicety

Decision-making is distributed across the stack and the roster with explicit authority boundaries. Before any reasoning begins, the Orchestrator queries the CDI Layer and emits the Capability Bundle — a snapshot of the reasoning frameworks available, the inference layers active, the cross-domain analogues relevant, and the Second Brain signal strength for the query class — so no agent reasons from a blank context. Mode selection follows: the Analyst declares Mode 1 and adapts a precedent if a strong prior returns, or declares Mode 2 and begins a derivation chain if none does; an artifact with no declared mode fails L1 validation. Because the mode determines which validation regime applies, the label is what lets the Diagnostic Agent and Statistician select the correct check automatically — the audit trail follows from the artifact itself, not from a reviewer's diligence.

The whole stack exists to make one arrow real: an L1 veto propagates straight to the decision output, bypassing every higher layer including the LLM.
Static five-layer inference-stack diagram: Forest Green for the L1 authority layer with a parchment panel body, the higher layers L2–L5 in neutral, and an amber focal treatment on the one veto arrow — L1 propagating straight to the decision output, bypassing every higher layer including the LLM. Exportable to a static PNG for the PDF and slide-deck formats.
Figure 8. The five-layer inference stack and its one non-negotiable arrow — a diagram of the architecture, not running software.

Five constraints are worth stating plainly. L1's veto scope is bounded to what it is programmed to catch — schema violations, known-bad patterns, named invariant checks — so a novel failure not yet typed into the L1 rule set can reach L5 before it is caught; L2 and L3 give probabilistic detection of degradation L1 misses, but those are signals, not veto conditions. Mode-declaration accuracy depends on agent discipline: an agent that mislabels a derivative analysis as first-principles breaks the audit trail without tripping a veto, because the mode field is required but its correctness is not deterministically validated. The Algorithmic Rule fires at the population level, not the individual investigation: the 10% applies across the pool of cycles, so a sustained run of routine queries can delay the exploration cadence while the Constraint Register accumulates hypotheses faster than the budget clears them — a named architectural tension. CDI Layer uptime is a load-bearing dependency targeted at ≥ 99.9%, a code-level guarantee in this single-operator build rather than a production SLA. And the practical depth of the seven modes varies with what has been demonstrated — Analogical and First-Principles are the most deeply exercised, and the system has not yet been run across arbitrary novel problem types invoking all seven at once under production conditions.

The measurable outcomes, all validated via simulation, show the framework working. The most direct evidence that the deterministic veto architecture works is the Phase 1 Storyteller record: the three L1 vetoes blocked 14 of 18 Storyteller runs during development, and one blocked run shows why the independence of the three checks matters — it reached 104 of 107 claims attributed (97.2% citation coverage) and passed the omission audit, and was stopped anyway because the causal-language veto found a single unsupported "due to". The report that was released cleared all three at 94.6% coverage, 88 of 93 claims — non-compliant outputs stopped before delivery, not flagged after. The Phase 4 ten-cycle run is the evidence for the Algorithmic Rule: a one-time 40–53% edit-distance step reduction across all three tracked query classes, then flat, with the rule firing on schedule and surfacing a non-obvious Constraint-Register hypothesis. Phase 5 is the evidence for the mode framework's differentiation: the "Spectral Coordination Sieve" was produced under First-Principles with a full derivation chain and passed Red-Team stress testing at Conditionally Robust. Phase 3 is the evidence for the Adversarial Game Trees and Counterfactual modes: three experiments analyzed blind produced NO_SHIP, HOLD_FOR_HARDENING, and SHIP verdicts without advance knowledge of which pathology each carried. Phase 6 is the evidence for human gating: the one Phase 7 proposal at the Confirmation Gate cannot auto-approve whatever its confidence or elapsed time. And Phase 2 is the evidence for Cross-Domain Analogy: all three injected failure classes detected, classified in domain-neutral terms, and autonomously remediated from the five analogue domains.

Recommendation

For a technical hiring manager or engineering leader: read this section as the answer to the right question. The question is not "does the system make good analytical decisions?" but "how does it prevent bad ones?" — and the answer is structural: a five-layer stack with deterministic L1 veto authority, a seven-mode framework that forces declaration of the generative process in every artifact, and a hard-coded exploration budget that keeps capability from plateauing together form a decision architecture whose governance is embedded in the design rather than imposed on top of it.

For an organization weighing the approach: the value of a layered inference stack is not any single analytical capability it enables, but the class of failures it structurally prevents. When an analytics system scales — more investigations, more agents, more sources — the governance surface scales with it, and an architecture that enforces correctness by construction scales differently from one that enforces it by convention. At ten investigations a week the difference is marginal; at a thousand it is architectural.
