All three tracked query classes showed the required one-time reduction as the first exemplar entered each class, the exploration-budget rule fired at cycle ten as specified against a non-obvious open hypothesis, and the compounding curve rendered to the design-token palette.

1.5 — A test-harness bug that masked the real categorization accuracy. The first Phase 4 categorization run reported accuracy at 17%. The number was wrong — the harness paired categorized telemetry triples with their expected categories positionally, and the two orderings did not line up, so it was scoring mismatched pairs. Fixing the harness to look each decision up by its triple identifier rather than by position revealed the real floor: 50%. I treat this as one of the more important entries in this section, because a harness that lies to the operator about pass rates is a worse failure than an honest pass-rate drop — it short-circuits the entire fix-it-and-log-it loop by hiding the very problems that loop exists to surface. The corrected 50% floor is what drove a real reordering of the promotion-gate rule set: strong rule-language signals moved ahead of the numeric-token check, an over-eager digit heuristic was replaced with a precise symmetric-difference token comparison, a bare "should" signal that mis-fired on ordinary sentences was dropped, and local-exception phrasing was inserted ahead of the numeric check. Categorization then reached 100%, with the generalizable exemplars auto-promoted and the ambiguous one quarantined exactly as the generalizable-class-only promotion rule requires.

1.6 — A three-failure calibration loop in the Phase 2 self-healing run. The first end-to-end Phase 2 run failed three different ways in succession, each fix exposing the next. First, a key collision in the Healing Agent's strategy projection, because the field that recorded strategies-evaluated was iterating over attempt records whose names had diverged; I split the projection into an explicit "queued" versus "tried" pair, which the Diagnostic-to-Healing handoff needs anyway, because that typed artifact serves two audiences — the audit trail and the replay. Second, the monitored-column name was being lost on the call stack between applying a repair and verifying it, so verification computed a row-count drift proxy instead of the column-level drift it had been asked for; I threaded the column identifier all the way through the apply-and-verify chain, since a verification that silently measures something other than what was authorized is precisely a no-deviation violation. Third, and most conceptually interesting, the classifier escalated a fully healed, nominal signal to operator review because it had no way to represent success — the escalation ladder has a "nominal" rung, but without an explicit no-failure short-circuit the classifier always fell into "best guess at which failure class this is," which is always wrong when there is no failure. I added that short-circuit at the top of the classifier. Alongside the code, the failure injections themselves had to be tuned so the synthetic signatures were actually detectable-but-not-trivial: the structural break was strengthened until its drift score cleared the first severity rung, and the gradual degradation was re-shaped to a gentle linear ramp so its drift shape is caught while its individual values stay in bounds — the canonical slow-degradation signature. I also narrowed the structural-break rule to require both elevated drift and a row-count jump, because high drift without a row-count change is gradual by definition. Finally, because a single-table monitor cannot see a cross-table dependency, I added cascade aggregation at the runner level: when two companion checks both fire, the runner synthesizes a cascade-class diagnostic for the healing handoff — the lowest-cost composition that respects each agent's single-realm contract rather than coupling the agents or adding a premature detector. On the next run all five Phase 2 exit criteria passed: three of three failures detected, classified, and autonomously remediated using cross-domain repair strategies, each with its minimum causal chain logged and its audit trail replayable.

1.7 — A Brittle framework on the first Forge run, and the right place to fix it. The first end-to-end Phase 5 run produced a novel detection framework that the Red-Team Agent rated Brittle — the proposed test had no adversary cost, since an attacker could slightly decorrelate timing and dissolve the detected signal at near-zero coordination overhead — and the pre-screen gate parked it, leaving the Conditionally-Robust exit criterion unmet. The important judgment here is that the Brittle verdict was correct: the framework genuinely was brittle, and the system's own risk register warns that a Red-Team which returns Robust on every test is not trying hard enough. So I fixed upstream of the verdict, not the verdict. I gave the invention engine richer cross-domain context — the full structural detail of each analogue rather than only its name — so it could choose a structurally relevant approach instead of a name-matched one, and I extended the Red-Team's stress test to decompose adversary cost into coordination complexity and campaign-efficiency loss, which made its verdicts honest about cost-of-evasion rather than mere possibility-of-evasion. The second run produced a genuinely novel framework whose primary weakness carried a medium coordination cost, which is a Conditionally Robust verdict rather than Brittle, and it was promoted to shadow evaluation. I rejected the alternatives that would have manufactured a pass — re-prompting the engine to "try harder," or lowering the Red-Team's bar so the first framework slipped through — because the second is exactly the false-confidence failure the risk register exists to prevent.

1.8 — An over-aggressive Red-Team verdict, and a fix I rejected before accepting a better one. In a partial Phase 3 run the Red-Team Agent rated one experiment Brittle on the basis of generic theoretical concerns about a metric class, with no experiment-specific evidence. The first proposed remedy was a calibration clause in the Red-Team's own prompt that would downgrade ungrounded Brittle verdicts — and I rejected that edit, correctly, because a prompt clause that amounts to "be less Brittle" is precisely the failure mode the risk register warns against: the Red-Team gets weaker and the system gains false confidence. The remedy I accepted instead preserves Red-Team severity while requiring an evidential basis: a rule that a Brittle verdict must point to a concrete, experiment-specific attack path rather than a concern that could be raised about any experiment of its type; a corrected mapping so that Brittle-without-a-sample-ratio-problem lands at hold-for-hardening rather than no-ship, and a clean statistical case can still ship at a Conditionally Robust verdict; and the artifact-type fix noted above. This is a positive-evidence requirement, not a verdict softener — the Red-Team can be as aggressive as it likes, but "Brittle" now has to mean "I found a specific weakness in this artifact," not "I am uneasy about this class of artifact." With those fixes all seven Phase 3 exit criteria passed, the three experiments resolved to their correct and distinct verdicts, and the not-all-Robust property held live.

1.9 — Seven compatibility fixes for a new evidence shape, and a protocol violation I logged against myself. A Storyteller briefing for a Phase 3 experiment failed five times in a row on a chain of seven separate compatibility issues, each fix exposing the next: a variable-name error, a false causal veto on a limitation statement that used "due to" in a data-availability sense, unrecognized experiment vocabulary in the readiness checklist, a chart-type whitelist that omitted the framings Phase 3 naturally uses, missing financial keywords in the significance signals, and citation-scope rules that were counting meta fields as if they were stakeholder prose. The common root cause was that the Storyteller had been hardened against Phase 1 evidence shapes, and Phase 3 evidence carries different vocabulary and chart structures; generalizing the keyword and chart-type sets to recognize the new shapes preserved every L1 semantic guarantee while extending the implementation. The sixth run passed at full citation coverage with all eighteen required assets. I record one more thing against this entry honestly: the session that did this work had its context fill and compact before its mandatory session-end documentation was written, which is a protocol violation under my own rules, and I logged it as one. The recovery is described in Section 4.

Section 2 · L1 governance intercepts

The L1 deterministic veto layer is the system's hard wall against the Storyteller publishing implied causation, uncited claims, omitted findings, or off-design visual output; its vetoes are non-overridable by the language-model layer above them. In Phase 1 alone the Storyteller iterated through 18 development runs — 14 of them blocked — before clearing all three checks. This section documents each intercept.

2.1 — Causal-language false positives in the Phase 1 Storyteller. The first live Phase 1 investigation ran successfully in 288.9 seconds and produced a discovery report and a stakeholder-briefing draft — and then the Storyteller's causal-language veto blocked its own output. The problem was not that the narrative made unsupported causal claims; it was that a substring matcher flagged the phrase "due to" wherever it appeared, including in sentences that describe statistical methodology, report a confidence score, state a proportional attribution, or narrate the reasoning process itself. I rewrote the check to read sentence-level context and exempt methodology, confidence, and reasoning-process language, and later upgraded the scan to a word-boundary match so it stopped catching "due to" inside unrelated words. The veto exists to stop the Storyteller from publishing causation the upstream analysis never established — a real constraint in this correlational domain — not to stop it from explaining its own methods, and every fix preserved that guarantee while removing the false positive. I rejected the tempting alternatives on principle: moving the check up to the language-model layer would have made it overridable, which the inference stack forbids, and hand-editing the narrative to delete "due to" would have violated the no-deviation rule and turned the Storyteller into a paraphraser when its mandate is faithful translation. The run that reached 97.2% citation coverage — 104 of 107 claims sourced, omission audit passed — was itself blocked by this veto over a single "due to", which is the clearest demonstration available that the three checks are independent and that clearing two is not a pass. A later run cleared all three at 94.6% coverage, and no subsequent phase has produced a causal false positive.

2.2 — Closing the Phase 1 citation-coverage gap. The first Phase 1 run cited about a tenth of its factual claims against an 80% requirement — the model wrote fluent narrative but, given a prompt with no explicit citation instructions or worked examples, few attributions. Successive runs surfaced three more distinct failures: the check was scanning the full model output, including methodology and metadata, rather than the stakeholder-facing section; its proximity window was too tight for dense financial paragraphs, so real citations sat just too far from the numbers they supported; and the model had no sanctioned way to cite an analyst estimate for a derived projection, so it either omitted projections or left them unattributed. I closed these in sequence — rewriting the citation rule with correct, wrong, and blocked worked examples; scoping the check to the stakeholder prose; adding a string-level fallback so a cited paragraph counts its claims as covered; sanctioning the analyst-estimate source with a placement rule to cite immediately after each number; and finally moving to numbered footnote markers backed by a validated footnote registry, where every marker must resolve to a footnote and every footnote to a recognized source. That last format change was deliberate: inline source tags next to each number are traceable but leak methodology into the narrative layer, whereas numbered footnotes keep the executive prose clean while preserving full citation integrity. Coverage climbed run over run to the 94.6% — 88 of 93 claims attributed — that the rest of this case study cites. I rejected loosening the check, since the gate exists to enforce the standard rather than to certify whatever the model produced, and rejected auto-inserting markers, since synthesizing attributions is derivation, which the Storyteller is forbidden to do. The pattern has held since; the Phase 3 briefing reached full citation coverage once its vocabulary was recognized.

2.3 — Executive-layer rules and a readiness checklist for the stakeholder briefing. The first live stakeholder briefing passed the existing L1 checks and still was not shippable: it buried its finding behind setup, carried inline statistical notation and artifact identifiers in the executive prose, put source tags and technical parameters in the primary recommendation, and had no explicit comprehensibility checkpoints. None of those were misleading-claim failures, so no existing veto caught them — they were executive-comprehensibility failures, and the dual-layer output standard is itself a Design Invariant. Rather than add manual review, which the proposal-rate-versus-capacity rule makes unsustainable, or a model self-check, which would be both overridable and circular, I added deterministic checks at the same authority level: an executive-layer rule that enforces a finding-first opening and keeps notation, identifiers, and technical parameters out of the executive layer, and a six-point readiness checklist covering comprehension, actionability, narrative structure, legibility, visual communication, and executive readiness. The required-asset set expanded to eighteen — adding the footnote registry, an external-dependencies list, and an auto-populated revision log that extends the audit trail through each iteration — and a technical annex was added to the schema so technical detail has a home outside the primary recommendation. A small static test suite verifies each rule fires on its injected failure mode. The briefing took real iteration to clear this harder gate, which is the gate working rather than failing; the same executive-layer discipline later carried to the Phase 3 briefing, and the checklist subsequently grew a seventh criterion for visual-design conformance.

2.4 — A runtime visual-conformance veto in the Diagnostic Agent. Writing a binding visual design system did not, by itself, make it load-bearing — agents and renderers could still drift from it. I closed that gap by giving the Diagnostic Agent a conformance check that runs on every stakeholder-briefing emission and scans the actual rendered output, markup and embedded charts alike, for off-palette colors, generic non-narrative chart titles, and decorative gradients or shadows, failing the envelope-level check on any violation. I put the veto in the Diagnostic rather than the Storyteller deliberately, to keep the produce-versus-validate separation intact and because a producer's self-check on visual conformance would be overridable in exactly the way the inference stack forbids. A pre-render lint would also have missed the point, since palette violations can be introduced at chart-render time, not just at specification time — only a scan of the finished output catches what the operator will actually see. The check has been a permanent link in the gate chain since; reusing its approved-color set immediately turned up sixteen off-palette values in the operator-console mockup, all fixed in the same session.

2.5 — The omission audit as a standing protection. The third of the Storyteller's L1 checks has never fired, and I document it here precisely because that is the correct state for it. It verifies that every finding the reviewer flags as material actually appears in the output, and blocks the report if any is missing. Its value is structural rather than incidental: the causal and citation vetoes cap what the Storyteller can say, and this one caps what it can omit, so the two together close the loophole where the easiest way to pass a hard citation or a cautious causal framing would be to drop the finding entirely. Without it, silence would be a tight narrator's path of least resistance; with it, that path is closed. It has stayed silent across every run to date, which is a backstop working as designed, not a check that is not needed.

Section 3 · Confirmation Gate intercepts

3.1 — The Phase 1 stakeholder briefing at the Confirmation Gate. The Phase 1 briefing — the 41-account coordinated-cluster finding — routed through the Confirmation Gate, which by invariant cannot auto-approve. I reviewed the self-contained HTML report in a browser, verified its conformance to the visual design system, and approved it for delivery, with the decision logged to the operational record. The reason this counts as a governance event rather than a formality is that Phase 1 could not exit without the sign-off, and the gate sat open for eight days while I rebuilt the HTML renderer across several sessions to meet the quality bar — the first renderer's output was, in my own note at the time, bad design. The gate did exactly what it is for: it blocked Phase 1 from closing until the artifact was actually shippable, and I declined the two shortcuts that would have closed it sooner — a timeout-based auto-approval, which the silence-is-not-approval rule forbids, and shipping a good-enough first version, which I rejected on quality. The delay paid off structurally, too, because it let the full visual design system land before Phase 2 rather than being retrofitted afterward.

3.2 — The self-generated Phase 7 proposal held at the gate. Phase 6's autonomous loop did what it was built to do: it identified a bottleneck in its own performance — the Statistician running overconfident on small subgroups — and generated a targeted improvement proposal, "Minimum-N Guard with Exact-Method Substitution," which passed its sandbox tests cleanly and routed itself to the Confirmation Gate as submitted-and-awaiting-decision. There it has stayed, with no auto-approval, because the gate never auto-approves. This is the single most important governance event in the build, and it is a success, not a stall: the strongest uncapped version of a self-improvement loop would let a system rewrite its own guardrails, and the no-auto-approve invariant together with the proposal-rate ceiling is exactly what separates recursive self-improvement from unsafe self-modification — the system may generate proposals freely but cannot adopt one without a human decision. The full cycle ran end to end, from telemetry through bottleneck identification, proposal, and sandbox test to the gate, with no adoption at the end of it. That the thing the gate is holding is the system's own proposal is the strongest test the property could face.

Section 4 · Compliance audits and directive violations

4.1 — A thirteen-item compliance-correction pass. A compliance audit surfaced thirteen gaps at once, spanning the knowledge vault's coverage, seven missing per-agent system prompts, two missing vault-write functions, a chart-linking parameter the vault writers did not accept, a filename-collision bug that let same-prefixed entries overwrite one another, and — most urgently — an API-key file sitting in the project root as a secret-exposure risk. Under the fix-it-and-log-it directive, a documented-but-uncorrected finding is not acceptable, so I ran the full remediation rather than noting it and moving on: I blanked the secret file and had the key rotated, wrote all seven agent prompts, added and wired the missing vault functions and the chart-linking parameter, fixed the collision with an identifier-suffixed filename pattern and a backfill that recovered the entries it had been silently overwriting, and wrote the missing governance, notification, artifact-type, and external-intelligence vault notes. One earlier deviation — a batch of vault entries written directly rather than through the canonical interface — I logged as an accepted deviation rather than rewrite, because the content already matched the specification exactly and the rewrite would have been a no-op. Two items that depended on not-yet-built Phase 2 components I formally deferred with rationale rather than close prematurely. The pass wrote 47 vault entries in total and substantially closed the coverage requirement — and the secret-file item is the origin of the hard pre-publication check that strips any key file before this work is ever made public.

4.2 — A context-compaction protocol violation, and the rule it produced. One session finished a Phase 3 stakeholder briefing and then had its context compacted by the system before the mandatory session-end documentation was written — with no proactive warning issued, in violation of the project's own most-important rule to flag context pressure before it forces a compaction. I treated it as a real violation rather than a near-miss, because the failure mode is structural: a compaction summary that says "resume directly" would, if followed, route the next session around the mandatory startup read and quietly perpetuate the drift. The recovery session reconstructed and logged both the lost work and the violation, and confirmed through a gap audit that nothing had actually been dropped. The lasting fix was a permanently locked override rule: a compaction summary is a context-reconstruction aid and cannot waive the session-start protocol, which takes unconditional precedence. Every session since has opened by reading its memory file regardless of what a summary instructs, and proactive context closure — warning before the window fills — became standard practice rather than an occasional courtesy.

4.3 — A documentation-drift correction pass, caught by this case study's own discipline. Five drift discrepancies surfaced while I was building the master prompt for this very case study. None affected system behavior — all were stale continuity-document claims that had fallen out of sync with what had actually been built and validated over the intervening sessions. A progress file contradicted itself, showing full completion in one table while still marking later phases as blocked in another and listing an already-closed blocker as open. A build-plan document still listed an early, partial version of the Phase 0 deliverables and exit criteria rather than the full set treated as authoritative elsewhere. A superseded model-identifier string lingered in two specification documents and — beyond the originally-scoped documentation fix — in a live configuration file, which made it a real config discrepancy rather than mere stale text. And two deeper conflicts I deliberately did not fix silently: a directives table in one document defined a near-opposite version of the governing directives, an early draft never reconciled, and the runtime prompt still specified sixteen required briefing assets against the eighteen-asset schema actually shipped. Those last two I surfaced for an explicit decision rather than resolve on my own, because choosing which of two contradicting authorities wins is a governance question, not a stale-fact correction, and the no-deviation rule requires authorization before reconciling sources against each other. The resolution confirmed the top-level instructions as the source of truth, the directives table was replaced to match, and the asset list was rewritten to the eighteen-asset schema. The revealing part is the discovery method: the drift was caught not by the system but by this case-study build, which carries a read-first grounding discipline — the same discipline the project's own primary-risk warning, that the primary risk is architectural drift caused by inadequate context preservation, exists to enforce. That discipline is now a permanent practice for these artifact builds.

Section 5 · Visual design system enforcement events

5.1 — A control-flow bug that left a chart empty. The first re-render under the redesigned chart renderer produced the eighteen-month abuse-trend chart with its structure intact but no data. The cause was a control-flow error: the renderer's lineage resolution — the step that finds the upstream evidence a chart draws from — was nested inside a conditional that only ran when a filename lookup keyed on one identifier succeeded, and when the chart was re-rendered by a different identifier that lookup returned nothing, so the lineage step never ran and the chart had no data to draw. A case-sensitive pattern match compounded it. I hoisted the lineage resolution out of the conditional so it runs regardless of which key found the file, and relaxed the match to be case-insensitive. Normalizing the stored lineage strings would have been the wrong fix, since the artifacts are immutable by design; the symmetric, lossless correction was at the renderer. The chart then drew its real trend.

5.2 — Hardcoded financial values in a stacked bar. A financial-impact chart was displaying approximate figures rather than the real numbers from the evidence bundle, and I flagged it on review — the chart was not showing the actual $5.89M Q1 total or its $1.52M coordinated-ring share. I replaced the hardcoded fallbacks with a real lookup from the evidence bundle, keeping a literal-value fallback only behind the primary path. A chart that estimates numbers the upstream analysis already computed both violates the no-deviation rule and breaks the design system's requirement that an insight callout naming a figure be backed by bars that actually sum to it. Corrected, the bar sums to the real total.

5.3 — A legend collision on the Pareto chart. The Pareto chart's legend sat where it overlapped a value label on the tallest bar. I moved it to the opposite corner rather than shrink either element below the design system's legibility floor. A small fix, recorded because that legibility floor is a hard constraint, not a preference.

5.4 — Dollar signs triggering math-mode in chart subtitles. The plotting library read the dollar signs in a subtitle as math delimiters and silently collapsed the spaces between them, mangling a phrase that named a dollar amount. I disabled math parsing on the title and subtitle text. Because dollar amounts are central to the financial narrative, a renderer that quietly eats whitespace inside them is producing wrong stakeholder output — worth a precise one-setting fix rather than escaping every dollar sign by hand.

5.5 — A color collision between Critical and Action states in the operator console. Mapping the operator console's five state colors onto the stakeholder palette's four collapsed Critical and Action onto the same amber, which broke the console's most basic job — telling a dangerous event apart from a routine action request at a glance — and the same audit found every state background sharing one parchment tone, so badges lost their figure-ground separation. The fix was a genuine scope decision rather than a tweak. I recognized that forcing the operator console through the stakeholder palette was a category error: the stakeholder palette is tuned for executive comprehension at low information density, while the console is tuned for state disambiguation at high density, and the two have different optimization targets. So I amended the design system's scope to govern stakeholder artifacts explicitly, exempted the single-operator console, and admitted one additional data-meaning color — a brick red reserved for the console's Critical state alone, which does not propagate to any stakeholder artifact. That satisfies the architecture's red-for-danger requirement for the console without weakening the finding-is-amber convention everywhere else. I rejected reusing one hue with icons for disambiguation, since console dashboards rely on at-a-glance hue distinction — the same reason traffic lights are universal — and rejected a near-amber shade for Action, since it would erode the amber convention. The cost, documented plainly, is that the single-system-wide-palette property now has two scopes, a boundary enforced by which files belong to which cluster. I also took the occasion to rewrite the console to a cleaner editorial layout across all six panels. Critical and action states now read apart at badge size, and the gate's plain-language summary sits above the fold with its decision controls kept in reach.

5.6 — A dark sidebar and a consistent icon set for the console. On review I wanted the console's sidebar to anchor navigation against the content, which the original light sidebar did not, and I noticed a stray hourglass emoji among an otherwise geometric icon set. I scoped a set of dedicated dark-sidebar variables so the change stayed entirely within the sidebar and left the content area untouched, and swapped the emoji for a geometric mark that is also semantically right — a focal-point glyph for the item needing attention rather than a decorative emoji. I kept the console's light content rather than take the whole interface dark, which was my preference, and the amber attention badge still reads cleanly against the darker sidebar.

Sources (Appendix A, Sections 1–5): the project change-tracker log; the operational (Mode A) log and phase-progression file; the two session-continuity files; the agent, library, and renderer code paths; the artifact and knowledge-vault store; and the visual design system.

Section 6 · Architectural constraint discoveries

These are the entries where a runtime problem turned out to be an architecture-level constraint rather than a local bug — the cases where fixing the immediate symptom meant getting a structural decision right.

6.1 — The cross-domain intelligence layer is always-on, not per-task. An early implementation treated the cross-domain intelligence layer as a per-task mechanism — built, queried once, and discarded — when the specification defines it as a continuously operating, system-wide layer. Correcting that was not a tidy-up; it was the difference between two architectures. Once the layer is always-on, three things become possible that a per-task version cannot support: the hard rule that any agent producing output without a recorded intelligence-layer query in its lineage is a validation failure becomes enforceable rather than vacuous; the layer can log which knowledge domains were queried, which were available but not, and which capabilities were exercised, which is the audit trail that later made the system's self-diagnosis of its own bottleneck possible; and external evidence registered during a research cycle propagates to every later task rather than only the one that fetched it. The per-task version would have been simpler, with no cross-task state to maintain, and I rejected it precisely because the audit-trail and knowledge-propagation guarantees both require persistence. The bottleneck the system later found in its own performance was detectable only because telemetry aggregated across sessions — which a per-task layer could never have retained.

6.2 — The Phase 1 signal is concentration, not volume — and that is an architectural finding. Phase 1's first investigation was meant to demonstrate detection of a coordinated abuse cluster, and the obvious expected result would have been a Q1 volume spike. The data showed the opposite: the Q1 abuse-event rate ran at 0.946 times the rest of the period — slightly below average, not a spike. The real signal was concentration. A small set of coordinated accounts, well under one percent of the population, produced about a fifth of the quarter's policy-violation events, and the wider forty-one-account ring ran at 16.54 times the surrounding population's rate. I record this among the architectural discoveries rather than the analytical results because of what it proves about the design: a population-level rate monitor — the standard dashboard signal — would have shown nothing wrong with Q1, and only graph analysis of account-level behavior surfaced the ring. It validated the acceptance criterion that the dataset must carry clusters detectable by graph analysis but not by naive thresholds, and it forced the executive-narrative rules to articulate concentration versus volume in plain stakeholder language rather than statistical notation. The pattern carried $5.89M of Q1 financial impact, and I registered the general principle as an open constraint: small coordinated clusters can create significant exposure while staying invisible to population-level monitors.

6.3 — Agents could read the knowledge vault but not write to it. The Orchestrator's mandate to query the knowledge vault before every task was working, but its counterpart — that every artifact emission produces a corresponding vault entry — was not, because no agent had a write path. Every run was leaving orphaned artifacts that existed in the store but never linked into the institutional knowledge graph, which turns the vault into a museum rather than a memory. I wrote a canonical vault-write interface with a function per output type, each producing an entry that opens with a one-line summary, carries a provenance block, and links to every related component, and wired it into each agent's emission step, then backfilled the entries that had been missed. I rejected having the operator write entries by hand (unscalable and itself a process violation), a separate vault-writer agent (write paths belong with the producing agent), and auto-deriving entries from the artifact record (the entries need a natural-language summary and relationship links the envelope does not carry). The lasting rule this established — no agent may produce an artifact without a corresponding vault write through the canonical interface — is one of the project's hard conventions, and it made the vault-coverage requirement achievable rather than perpetually behind.

6.4 — Single-operator capacity, and metrics that secretly needed judgment. The early architecture assumed an always-available operator with unbounded review capacity, and an audit found several metrics that gated phase transitions while carrying hidden judgment dependencies the system could not resolve on its own. Both are expressions of the same reality — there is exactly one operator — and I addressed them together. I added explicit single-operator operating constraints: a review-queue capacity ceiling, team-expansion triggers, and a rule that self-improvement proposal generation throttles when the queue exceeds the ceiling, so the system cannot generate a thousand proposals at one human. And I required every metric to be assigned, before deployment, to one of three handling mechanisms — deterministic auto-resolution, an operator-approved deterministic rule, or an escalation flag for the ones that genuinely need judgment at runtime — with a Phase 0 exit criterion that no unresolved judgment-bound metric may sit in a gate-triggering category. The reasoning is that a metric requiring judgment at gating time would either block the gate forever or silently auto-pass, both pathological; forcing resolution to a deterministic mechanism before a phase deploys keeps the gate operable, while flagging the genuinely-judgment-bound ones as escalations keeps the gate from lying about its own certainty. I rejected the shortcut of auto-approving after a timeout in single-operator mode, because silence is not approval. The capacity ceiling is not theoretical — it is exercised live in the Phase 6 self-proposal flow.

6.5 — Natural language, not SQL, is the default interface. The conventional analytics-engineering pattern would have agents emit SQL as their primary output, and the early architecture assumed as much before the specification locked SQL down to a subordinate, explicitly-invoked, sandboxed execution capability, with the default interface being natural language to execution plan to result. There are three reasons this is the right constraint. A SQL query is not a stakeholder artifact, so a SQL-first agent has to translate its output into the plain-language layer, adding a translation step that can drift from what actually ran. Metrics in this system are defined in a governed semantic layer rather than in ad-hoc SQL, and an agent emitting raw SQL can quietly bypass those definitions. And confining SQL execution to a sandbox makes the security boundary explicit rather than diffuse. I rejected both SQL-first agents and a mixed mode where some agents lead with SQL, the latter because inconsistency is its own liability. No agent has emitted SQL as a primary output across any phase.

6.6 — A ten-percent exploration budget the system cannot skip. The specification hard-codes an exploration rule: roughly every tenth investigation cycle is redirected to a counter-intuitive hypothesis drawn from the open-questions register, the operator may tune the percentage within a bounded band, and the system itself cannot skip these cycles or set the rate to zero. This is the design's anti-plateau mechanism, and the specification's own illustration — a capability that plateaus after fifty cycles without the rule versus compounding far higher with it — is a target justified by cross-domain analogy, not a magnitude measured in this simulation, and I keep it labeled as such. I implemented it with a persistent counter that survives across sessions, a firing decision based on how far behind the expected exploration count the system has fallen (so a short session cannot quietly skip its obligation — the backlog simply fires later), selection of the least-used open question, and a fallback to the intelligence layer's non-activation log if the register is ever empty, because the cycle must fire regardless. I rejected a soft suggestion to explore (the rule's whole purpose is structural — to counter the system's natural tendency to converge on its own priors), a fixed every-Nth cadence (session length varies, so a rate-based trigger is more robust), and any option to set exploration to zero (a hard floor forbids it). In the Phase 4 demonstration it fired exactly once across ten cycles, on schedule, against a genuinely non-obvious hypothesis.

Section 7 · Process and protocol changes triggered by incidents

This section is about the build process rather than the system. The continuity protocol that lets a single-operator project span dozens of sessions was not designed up front; it accreted, each rule added in response to a specific incident.

7.1 — Narrowing the mandatory session-start read to one file. The session protocol originally required reading three continuity files at the start of every session — well over a hundred thousand tokens of consumption before any work began, so sessions started already heavily loaded. I narrowed it: the persistent memory file is now the only mandatory start read, while the progress tracker and change log stay mandatory session-end updates but are read on demand rather than always. The memory file was already designed to be the context layer of record, so reading the other two on top of it was double-counting most of what it already summarizes. I rejected compressing all three into one file (they serve different audit purposes) and reading only the most recent change-log entries (the heuristic for what counts as recent would itself need maintenance). Every session since has had meaningfully more headroom for real work — this one included.

7.2 — A paste-and-resume starter message at every session close. When one session finished its code but deferred the demonstration, the next had to reconstruct the task state from scattered context — workable but slow. So I made a starter message mandatory at the close of every session: a self-contained, paste-ready block carrying the current phase and status, what the session completed, the ordered next-session task list, and any execution-environment notes, with non-compliance treated as a protocol violation. For a project that explicitly assumes it will outlast any single session, this is structural rather than cosmetic — it converts continuity from reconstruct-from-logs into paste-and-resume, and the producing session, which has the freshest context, is the right author. I rejected leaving it to the operator and auto-deriving it from the memory-file updates, which are summary-level and lack the explicit next-task scope the resume actually needs. Every session since has closed this way — and this appendix is being written under exactly that protocol.

7.3 — Extending the proactive-context rule to gradual load. The directive that governs context management originally covered a capacity check before a heavy task, but not the quieter failure where load accumulates gradually across many small tasks — which is exactly what caused an early silent compression. I extended it across the governing documents so that a session noticeably loaded from prior reads and writes must warn the operator before the next substantial task and offer a fresh-session starter, rather than wait for a compaction to fire. The reasoning is that compaction is lossy: once it triggers, the decisions and discoveries in the compacted span are summarized but no longer fully recoverable, so the proactive warning is the only point at which the operator can still choose to defer, close, or proceed before the loss is locked in. I rejected staying reactive-only (the failure kept recurring) and a hard cap on session size (too rigid — some long sessions run fine); the judgment call of "noticeably loaded" preserves the flexibility while catching the destructive case. This very session's repeated context checkpoints are that rule in operation.

7.4 — A locked rule that a compaction summary cannot override the protocol. A session once opened with a system-generated compaction summary instructing it to "resume directly," followed the instruction, and thereby skipped the mandatory startup read and capacity assessment — until I intervened. The fix was a permanently-locked rule at the top-level-instruction authority: a compaction summary is a context-reconstruction aid and does not waive the session-start protocol, which takes unconditional precedence. Otherwise the summary becomes a back door around governance, an auto-generated artifact quietly overriding an explicit operator policy. I rejected disabling compaction summaries (they are genuinely useful when used correctly) and treating the incident as a one-session correction (it would simply recur). Every session since — including this one, which opened on a fresh instruction and still read its memory file and stated its context status before any work — runs the protocol regardless of what any summary says.

Section 8 · Other notable design decisions and engineering events

8.1 — Revising the dataset scale so the signals were real. The initial dataset specification used fifty thousand API events over twelve months, and analysis showed that was too thin: a fifty-account coordinated cluster would be two and a half percent of the population — trivially detectable — and twelve months was too short for the slow-escalation detection the demonstration needed. I revised the scale to a default of seven hundred fifty thousand events over an eighteen-month horizon, controlled by a single proportional scale parameter so the whole dataset can be shrunk for development and restored for the final run. The point was acceptance-criteria integrity: at the small scale the coordinated-cluster pattern collapses into simple threshold detection, defeating the very thing Phase 1 exists to show, whereas at the larger scale the clusters sit in genuine hard-signal territory. I rejected running at five million events (generation time and storage exceeded any need) and kept downsampling only as a development convenience. The dataset generated at full scale in about twenty-five seconds with all five required signal patterns confirmed present, at the seven-table row counts this case study cites throughout.

8.2 — Bumping the pinned model under the "strongest available" clause. The portability wrapper pinned a specific model identifier, while the specification authorizes the strongest available frontier model of that family under an explicit "or strongest available" clause, so I updated the pin to the newer model. This is an application of the no-deviation rule, not a violation of it: the source says to use the strongest available, so continuing to pin the older identifier once a stronger one exists would have been the deviation. I rejected freezing the older model for reproducibility, because the reproducibility guarantee in this system lives at the immutable-artifact level, not the model level. The residual risk — that model behavior shifts subtly between versions — is caught where it would surface, at the deterministic output gates, and a later drift-correction pass cleaned up two stale references to the old identifier, one of them in a live configuration file rather than mere documentation.

8.3 — Making the innovation mandate stateful. One Design Invariant requires that at least a set fraction of first-principles invention cycles produce a genuinely novel result — a mandate that is unenforceable across sessions without persistent state. I added a state file that tracks first-principles cycles against the novel subset, with a grace period for the first couple of cycles, and a gate filter that blocks incremental refinement whenever the mandate is out of compliance. The reasoning is that the mandate is a lifetime property, not a one-cycle one: without accumulated state it collapses into "this single cycle was novel," which is trivially satisfiable and architecturally meaningless. I rejected manual operator tracking (unscalable and a bypass of automated governance) and recomputing the rate from the operational logs on every cycle (expensive, and it makes one corrupted log a single point of failure for the gate). In the Phase 5 demonstration the mandate held.

8.4 — Making the portability layer load-bearing. The architecture promises that a single abstraction wrapper is the seam at which the whole system could later migrate off its current orchestration onto a different agent framework, and Phase 6's job was to make that abstraction real rather than nominal. The original wrapper exposed only a single synchronous call, with no streaming, no extended-thinking capability flag, and no portability documentation. I added documentation of the three integration points a future migration will actually touch — tool-format differences, context-window limits, and extended-thinking availability — plus a streaming method that returns the same shape as the non-streaming call so downstream consumers need not branch, and a capability flag for the reasoning modes that use extended thinking. I documented the integration points now rather than at migration time because they are needed to plan the migration, not to execute it, and I kept the scope to "documented and alternatively invoked" rather than building a full second-provider adapter, which would have been out of scope for the phase. The demonstration exercised the streaming path and confirmed the capability flag, and the exit criterion was met.

8.5 — The Capability Bundle as the first artifact on every task. The Orchestrator's contract is to emit a Capability Bundle — a point-in-time snapshot of what the intelligence layer holds for this task — before any downstream agent begins, and Phase 6 was the first end-to-end test that the bundle correctly captures the exploration-rule state, the domains queried, the domains available but not queried, and the capabilities exercised. This is where the content-hash bug from the first section actually surfaced: the bundle must be immutable from the moment it is emitted, and the fix preserved both properties at once — first-artifact ordering and immutability. The bundle matters because it is the root of the audit trail; without it as the first artifact, the downstream validation checks have no baseline for what the system knew going into the task. In the demonstration the bundle carried the task decomposition, the exploration-rule state, and the intelligence-layer lineage, and it was consumed downstream by the bottleneck detector and the self-improvement proposer.

Section 9 · Cross-cutting observations

Five patterns run through every entry above, and they are the through-line I want a reader to leave with.

The fix-it-and-log-it directive is the system's quality-control engine. Nearly every entry in this appendix closes a finding by both correcting it and logging the correction, and the log entry then becomes the source for the next audit. The thirteen-violation remediation is the most visible instance, but the pattern recurs everywhere — a logged process violation, a locked override rule, a drift discovery escalated and resolved across three linked entries. Without that directive the system would carry a steady backlog of found-but-not-fixed issues; with it, every finding either closes or is explicitly deferred with acknowledged rationale.

The L1 vetoes catch real problems, which is why the calibration took as many runs as it did. The eight-run Phase 1 storyteller calibration and the six-run Phase 3 calibration can look like over-engineering until you notice the gates caught a genuine issue every time — and the false positives, like "due to" flagged in a methodology sentence, were as informative as the true ones, because each drove an implementation improvement that has held across later phases. The rule that L1 vetoes cannot be overridden is what kept the calibration honest; a relaxable gate would have stopped iterating at the first false positive and shipped lower-quality output.

Phase exit criteria are gates, not goals. Every phase carries lettered exit criteria, and a phase does not exit until all of them are met. The clearest demonstration is Phase 1 sitting at "gate signed" status for eight days while I rebuilt the visual layer to standard — "we will polish it in the next phase" was never on the table.

Three mechanisms together form a complete audit trail. The intelligence layer captures what the system knew, the Capability Bundle captures what it queried, and the operational log captures what it did — and the Phase 6 audit of 175 artifacts confirmed that traceability end to end. It is not a coincidence that the very first content-hash bug was caught by the audit trail's own integrity check running against a produced artifact.

Single-operator economics shape every architectural choice. There is one operator, and the no-auto-approve gate, the proposal-rate throttle, the review-queue ceiling, and even the split between the operator console's design language and the stakeholder artifacts' all flow from that one fact. Recognizing where a single audience at high information density needs different treatment from a stakeholder audience at low density was itself the engineering work.

The internal record closes with two reference tables — a change-tracker cross-reference mapping each build-change entry to the sections it appears in, and a consolidated list of key artifact identifiers for verification — which are scaffolding for a fact-checker with access to the internal record rather than narrative content, so they are kept in the internal record rather than reproduced here.

Sources (Appendix A, Sections 6–9, and the internal reference tables): the project change-tracker log and its cross-reference table; the persistent memory file and phase-progression file; the first-investigation postmortem; the constraint register; the agent, library, orchestration, and telemetry code paths; the semantic layer; the governance configuration; the artifact and knowledge-vault store with its verification-identifier set; and the architecture and build-plan specifications. This block complements the Sections 1–5 sources above; together they cover the whole appendix.

B Appendix B · Phase engineering history The engineering value of a phased build was in what each phase's hardest choices made possible two and three phases later

A first-person record of the build's phase-by-phase engineering history — the companion to Appendix A. Where Appendix A catalogs what broke at runtime and how each fix was made, this appendix is organized by build phase, zero through six, and asks a different question of each one: why the phase was designed the way it was, what hard problems its design had to navigate, and what its engineering work made possible in the phases that followed. Each phase is examined through the same six lenses — its charter, its engineering challenges, its major design decisions, the constraints that shaped it, the lessons it produced, and its cross-phase influence — and every claim traces to a specific change-tracker entry, build-plan section, postmortem, or artifact identifier in the internal record.

The engineering value of a phased build is not concentrated in any single phase — it is in what each phase's hardest architectural choices made possible, or prevented, two and three phases later.

A system-wide intelligence layer chosen over a simpler per-task one, artifacts made immutable and content-hashed from the first schema, a synthetic dataset engineered so its signal is concentration rather than volume — each of these cost more than the obvious alternative at the time, and each turned out to be exactly what a later phase's capability depended on. This appendix traces that compounding, phase by phase, and that is the reason it is worth reading alongside the runtime catalog: the runtime record shows the guardrails firing, and this record shows why the structure behind them was built the way it was.

Maldros was built in seven sequential phases, zero through six, each a hard prerequisite for the next, with no parallel tracks in the single-operator build. Every phase carried lettered exit criteria that had to be met in full before the next phase could open — they are gates, not goals — and the discipline of never crossing a gate until it is genuinely met is what let the early architectural choices stay load-bearing rather than being quietly relaxed under schedule pressure. I organize the record by phase here, rather than by issue type, because the story I want a reader to follow is not what broke but why each phase was shaped the way it was and what it handed forward.

The division of labor between this appendix and Appendix A is deliberate. If you want to know what failed at runtime and how it was fixed, Appendix A is the exhaustive catalog; if you want to know why a phase's design took the form it did and how its decisions propagated, this is that account. The source discipline is identical to Appendix A's — every claim below traces to a specific change-tracker entry, build-plan section, postmortem, or artifact identifier in the internal record — and, as there, I have kept those internal identifiers out of the narrative and preserved them in the internal record, so the prose stays readable while remaining fully checkable.

Phase 0 · Foundation

The charter. Phase 0 had to produce everything the system would need before the first agent ever fired — not analytical output, but the infrastructure that would make all analytical output trustworthy. The build plan was explicit that this phase produces no analytical output and instead produces the infrastructure that makes all analytical output trustworthy, and it set thirteen numbered deliverables against nine lettered exit criteria. The deliverables spanned the whole foundation: the synthetic dataset, the semantic-layer metric definitions, the initial population of the knowledge vault, the artifact schema definitions, the Orchestrator prototype, a working Python execution environment, the cross-domain intelligence layer infrastructure, the operator configuration, the judgment-metric registry, a dataset-review workflow, the notification mechanism, the Confirmation Gate stub, and an operator-interface mockup for review. None of these produces a finding; every one of them is what makes a later finding auditable.

Engineering challenges. The hardest problem in Phase 0 was not generating data — it was generating data that was analytically non-trivial. The plan warned in as many words that the quality of every demonstration in the phases that followed depends entirely on the quality of the synthetic dataset, and that a dataset that is random, thin, or internally inconsistent would produce analyses that look mechanical and fail to demonstrate genuine reasoning. The core tension was that the signal patterns had to be detectable by the system's actual analytical methods — graph clustering, sequential-probability-ratio testing for slow escalation, distribution-drift monitoring — but not trivially obvious from naive inspection: a coordinated abuse cluster visible from a simple volume spike would be pedagogically hollow, while one visible only from graph-level concentration and invisible at the population level validates real analytical work. That balance is a scale problem as much as a design one. The initial dataset was fifty thousand API events, and at that scale a coordinated cluster of fifty accounts is two and a half percent of the account population — trivially detectable. The insight that resolved it was that coordinated clusters have to sit in hard-signal territory, detectable by graph analysis but not by naive thresholds, which requires both the cluster and its background to be large enough that concentration, not raw volume, is the signal; at three-quarters of a million events across eighteen months, nineteen labeled cluster accounts — under one percent of two thousand — generating a fifth of the quarter's policy-violation events at roughly twenty-one times per-account concentration is a genuine finding rather than a toy example. A subtler challenge was architectural: an early implementation treated the cross-domain intelligence layer as something built and queried once per task and then discarded, when the specification defines it as a continuously operating, system-wide layer. The per-task version is much simpler and looked sufficient for Phase 0's own exit criteria; the difference only surfaces two and four phases later, when cross-session telemetry aggregation and the system's self-diagnosis of its own bottleneck both turn out to require state a per-task layer would have thrown away — so Phase 0 had to make the harder choice without yet having the evidence that it mattered. And all of this had to happen while standing up functional governance — a Confirmation Gate stub, a notification mechanism, a judgment-metric registry, an interface mockup — where "functional" meant actually triggering, routing, and refusing to auto-approve, not merely documented; delivering thirteen deliverables and nine exit criteria in the earliest sessions was itself a context-management problem.

Design decisions and rationale. Five decisions shaped the phase. The dataset scale was revised from fifty thousand events over twelve months to a default of seven hundred fifty thousand over eighteen — January 2024 through June 2025 — because the five required signal patterns demanded it: gradual safety-bypass escalation needs enough temporal resolution for sequential testing to distinguish a slow ramp from noise, the three pipeline-failure types need distinct temporal signatures, and regulatory events that lag-correlate to internal abuse patterns need eighteen months to show a meaningful lag; a scale parameter was added so development runs could use a fraction of the data without regenerating the whole set. The cross-domain intelligence layer was fixed as the continuously maintained source of truth, with the per-task Capability Bundle redefined as a point-in-time snapshot of it and the hard rule that an agent producing output with no recorded intelligence-layer query in its lineage is a diagnostic-level failure — a decision with three downstream consequences that only appeared later: cross-session bottleneck detection, external-evidence propagation through the research loop, and a non-activation log that became the data source for that bottleneck analysis. Artifact immutability was set in the schema definitions themselves: every hand-off is a JSON artifact written once, content-hashed, and never edited in place, with corrections producing a new versioned artifact that references the original — the rule whose existence is exactly why a later write-after-hash mutation in Phase 6 was caught rather than silently absorbed, because a content-stable artifact is the only thing the diagnostic envelope check can soundly audit. The judgment-metric registry required every analyst-judgment-bound metric to be resolved ahead of time to one of three mechanisms — deterministic auto-resolution, an operator-approved deterministic rule, or an escalation flag — with the escalation-flag class barred from gating a phase transition or triggering the Confirmation Gate, because a metric that needs human judgment at gate-check time either blocks the gate forever or silently auto-passes, and both are pathological. And the single-operator capacity constraints corrected the architecture's original, wrong assumption of an always-available operator with unbounded review capacity, adding a review-queue ceiling, four team-expansion triggers, and proposal-rate throttling once the queue exceeds the ceiling — the architecture that later became the proposal-rate-below-review-capacity invariant that keeps the Phase 6 self-improvement loop from ever overwhelming the one human in the loop.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Four constraints bounded the work. The first is that the data-generation tool is not a warehouse: a seeded Python generator (numpy/pandas) builds and exports the synthetic dataset to Parquet, but it has no live query API, no schema-contract enforcement, and no drift monitoring, so the monitoring agent introduced later cannot query it directly and instead watches its file outputs, and the semantic layer is a set of YAML definitions rather than a live semantic engine. That single fact propagates through every downstream choice — columnar Parquet exports as the canonical format, an in-memory DuckDB engine reading those files, Python for analysis — because the file, not a database connection, is the data contract. The second is that simulation is not production: the dataset is deterministic, seeded, and synthetic, real-world patterns will be noisier and real clusters less cleanly bounded, and the plan documents this as a known ceiling on the demonstrations that follow, which are proofs of capability against a designed-for dataset rather than evidence of live performance. The third is spec completeness — the directive that every field, attribute, value, rule, and constraint in the source specification must be represented in the implementation, with partial implementation not permitted, which is why Phase 0 had to deliver all thirteen deliverables rather than the "important" subset. The fourth is the no-unauthorized-ideas directive: any new idea, design change, or approach not already in the source documents required explicit operator approval before implementation, so even small architectural variations — how to implement the intelligence-layer update path, for instance — were surfaced for a decision rather than silently resolved.

Lessons learned. Four lessons carried forward. The first is that dataset design is the most underestimated phase in any analytics build; the plan says so directly, and the Phase 1 finding that the cluster signal is concentration rather than volume validated it — the deliberate choice to embed three labeled clusters of eight, six, and five accounts at low absolute count but high per-account concentration is what gave Phase 1 anything interesting to find. The second is that scale rationale has to be settled before the first data-generation run, because a dataset too thin for a later phase's needs is not catchable at that later phase: re-running Phase 0 would invalidate every content-hashed artifact built against the original data. The third is that governance stubs must be functional rather than scaffolds — the notification and Confirmation Gate exit criteria required real triggering, routing, and no-auto-approve enforcement, so that every subsequent governance event ran against real infrastructure rather than a mock. The fourth is that the intelligence layer's continuously-running requirement is non-negotiable from Phase 0: correcting the per-task misread was far harder to contemplate in Phase 1, once agents had already been built against the wrong mental model, than it was to get right before any agent existed.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 0's decisions are visible in nearly every later phase. The scale revision directly determined Phase 1's central finding: at fifty thousand events the concentration-not-volume result would not have been non-obvious; at three-quarters of a million it required graph analysis to see at all. The intelligence layer's continuous architecture is what made Phase 4's research-loop evidence propagation possible and Phase 6's bottleneck detection achievable — without cross-session persistence, the small-subgroup overconfidence the system later diagnosed in itself could never have been assembled from aggregated operational logs. The artifact-immutability rule set in the schema definitions is what caught the Phase 6 content-hash mutation, a fix that was correct precisely because the rule was well established. And the judgment-metric registry together with the single-operator capacity constraints established the proposal-rate-below-capacity invariant that later kept the recursive self-improvement loop safe — the Phase 0 decision is what prevents a Phase 7 from becoming unsafe self-modification.

Phase 1 · First end-to-end demonstration

The charter. Phase 1 had to run one complete investigation from question to final deliverable — Orchestrator to Analyst to Statistician to Storyteller — producing a discovery report and a stakeholder briefing carrying all eighteen required assets. The question was pre-specified and pointed: was the Q1 rise in API-abuse volume driven by coordinated multi-account behavior or by organic growth, and if coordinated, what was the financial impact and the indicated countermeasure? Five deliverables — four working agent implementations, a complete discovery report, the eighteen-asset briefing, an artifact-lineage trace, and a postmortem — sat against an exit criterion stated in terms of two readers at once: a non-technical stakeholder must be able to understand the executive narrative without the technical layer, and a technical reviewer must be able to reproduce the finding from the discovery path alone.

Engineering challenges. The phase's challenges clustered around a single hard requirement: a genuinely dual-layer output from an agent forbidden to derive. The Storyteller's mandate is pure translation — it must produce both a technical discovery report and a plain-language executive narrative but cannot add a finding, a citation, or a datum not already present in the evidence it is handed — and every L1 veto it triggered was a calibration point on that constraint rather than a reasoning failure. The causal-language veto firing on a methodology sentence, and the citation-coverage check failing at roughly a tenth of the required attribution, were both gaps in how the gate was specified — an over-inclusive substring match, an instruction abstract enough to under-constrain the model — not defects in what the Storyteller was doing, and distinguishing a gate that was over-calling from one that was under-calling required running both across successive iterations. The Storyteller took 18 development runs to clear all three L1 checks — 14 of them blocked — and Appendix A carries the run-by-run detail; the design-level point is that the iteration was the only available mechanism, because an L1 veto is an absolute block with no "ship with warnings" path. A second challenge was that the Confirmation Gate delay exposed the visual layer: the briefing first reached ready-for-review status but sat unsigned for eight days, because the first HTML renderer's output was, in my own note at the time, bad design, and the no-auto-approve rule meant the phase could not exit on a report I was unwilling to certify as stakeholder-ready. Those eight days were not lost — they produced three renderer rewrites, a run of chart-calibration fixes, a five-layer visual enforcement architecture, a system-wide palette, and the visual design system's confirmation as a peer authority — all before Phase 2 began. A third challenge was an omission rather than a bug: after the first complete run, not one agent had written to the knowledge vault, because the write path had simply not been built yet, which violated the rule that information must not exist as isolated records and left the phase's artifacts to be backfilled by a separate script — the origin of the now-architecturally-enforced rule that no agent may emit an artifact without a corresponding vault write. And a fourth was narrower: the initial inline citation format was traceable but leaked methodology references into the executive narrative, which the numbered-footnote format introduced later resolved by separating citation integrity from narrative cleanliness.

Design decisions and rationale. Four decisions came out of the phase. The required-asset count for the stakeholder briefing expanded from fifteen to eighteen after the first briefing passed every existing check and still failed six structural rules no gate yet existed for — findings buried behind setup, statistical notation in executive prose, identifier leakage into the narrative, inline source markers in the recommendation, technical parameters in the primary recommendation, and no explicit comprehensibility checkpoint — so three new assets (a footnote registry, an external-dependencies list, and a revision log) and two new deterministic checks were added, each filling a specific governance gap rather than an aesthetic preference. The visual design system was established as a peer authority alongside the three specification documents, with its four-color palette, its finding-first communication pattern, and its chart-construction rules made permanently locked semantic guarantees; the behavioral rule that its amber marks exactly one thing per context — the finding — is load-bearing, and an early assignment that put amber on the non-finding bar was corrected precisely because amber has to mean "this is the finding," not "this is whatever the plotting library drew second." That system was then made load-bearing through five enforcement layers — central design tokens as the single source of truth, a mandatory session-start read before any visual work, a named file cluster that forces a full-cluster update on any visual change, a readiness-checklist criterion for conformance, and an intelligence-layer domain whose non-activation on a visual task is itself a failure — with the operationally important rule being that color, type, and layout tokens are never hand-edited in a consumer file but only in the token source. And the Analyst pipeline was fixed as hypotheses to data-query-through-the-semantic-layer to Python execution, with SQL confined to sandboxed execution rather than appearing as an agent's output, because a raw query is not a stakeholder artifact, emitting one can bypass the semantic layer's metric definitions, and keeping SQL in a sandbox clarifies the security boundary.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Four constraints defined what Phase 1 could and could not do. The Storyteller does not derive, only translates — an absolute rule that made the citation problem structurally hard, because the numerical claims it had to attribute were analyst-derived projections, and without a sanctioned way to cite an analyst estimate those projections would be either uncited or dropped; sanctioning that source type was the architectural solution, an expansion of what the Storyteller may cite, never of what it may derive. L1 vetoes cannot be overridden, so every check failure was an absolute block and the eight-run calibration was the only route to a passing state — there was no path to "ship with L1 warnings." No auto-approve holds under any condition, which is what turned the eight-day gate wait into the gate working rather than a process failure — the visual rebuild had to happen before Phase 2, not be retrofitted after it. And the dual-layer output standard is itself an invariant: both a technical and a plain-language layer must be present and independently readable, which is harder than being technically correct because it demands a genuinely different communication mode in the same document.

Lessons learned. The phase produced five lessons. The first is that L1 gates are calibration instruments, not pass/fail switches: the postmortem reads the eight-run calibration as the gates working — blocking an uncertified output rather than passing a non-compliant one — with each iteration improving the gate's specificity without weakening its coverage, and false positives a tuning problem rather than a governance failure. The second is that the Confirmation Gate delay was the best available outcome, because those eight days produced the entire visual design system and its enforcement layers before Phase 2 built the monitoring agent, which could then include visual conformance natively instead of retrofitting it. The third is that the vault's write path needs to exist before the first agent runs, since backfilling the first phase's entries was the symptom of building the write infrastructure after the agents were already producing artifacts. The fourth is the most analytically interesting: the Statistician challenged the investigation's own premise, finding that the Q1 abuse rate was slightly below the period average rather than elevated — directly contradicting the "spike" the question assumed — and the system documented that contradiction explicitly rather than fabricating support for the assumed spike, which is exactly what a trustworthy analytical system should do. The fifth is that worked examples in a system prompt drive model compliance: citation coverage moved from a tenth of claims under an abstract instruction to near-total under an instruction carrying correct, wrong, and blocked examples with a placement rule — showing the model what compliance looks like, not merely telling it.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 1's investment compounded forward on four tracks. The L1 veto's keyword exemptions and citation permissions carried into Phase 3, where the Storyteller's different evidence vocabulary needed a further round of compatibility fixes — but the framework was already there and the calibration was incremental, not a rebuild. The visual design system installed during the gate delay was built natively into Phase 2's monitoring agent as a conformance veto, so Phase 2 never had to retrofit it. The vault write path was extended in every subsequent phase — diagnostic and healing writers in Phase 2, few-shot and rule writers in Phase 4, an invention writer in Phase 5, bottleneck and proposal writers in Phase 6 — the architecture established once and extended each time. And the Confirmation Gate precedent — wait for sign-off, never auto-approve, do not ship until the artifact is genuinely stakeholder-ready — set the operational pattern used unchanged through Phase 6's held self-generated proposal.

Phase 2 · Self-healing data lifecycle

The charter. Phase 2 introduced the Diagnostic and Healing agents and had to show that the system could detect, diagnose, and autonomously remediate data-quality failures with a complete, replayable audit trail. Five deliverables — the Diagnostic Agent, the Healing Agent, three synthetic failure scenarios, a maximum-capacity escalation condition, and a root-cause-analysis protocol — sat against exit criteria that were unusually specific: all three injected failures detected, correctly classified, and remediated autonomously, each with its minimum causal chain logged and its audit trail replayable, and the human not called until all six maximum-capacity conditions held at once.

Engineering challenges. Three challenges dominated. The first was failure-injection calibration: the synthetic failures had to be both detectable by the monitoring agent's drift thresholds and representative of real failure signatures, and the first injection parameters produced drift readings below the first severity rung — so they had to be tuned, the structural break strengthened until its drift score cleared the rung, and the gradual degradation re-shaped into a gentle linear ramp whose values stay within absolute bounds. That gradual case was the hardest precisely because its whole point is to be missed by naive threshold monitors: its drift shape is anomalous while its individual values are not, which is the canonical slow-degradation signature. The second challenge was that a cascade failure crosses table boundaries the monitoring agent is contractually forbidden to cross — its mandate is to watch one data realm at a time, but a cascade is null values propagating from one table into another, which requires comparing signals across two. The resolution was deliberately not a new agent, which would have added a unit boundary without changing the work, but synthesis at the runner level: when two independent single-realm checks both fire, the runner composes a cascade-class diagnostic for the healing hand-off, which respects each agent's single-realm contract while recovering cross-table detection at the orchestration layer. The third challenge surfaced when the stakeholder palette was applied to the operator console and collapsed its critical and action states onto the same amber — a dashboard that renders its most dangerous alert and a routine request identically is functionally broken. Resolving it meant recognizing a category error: the stakeholder palette is tuned for executive comprehension at low information density, while the console is tuned for state disambiguation at high density, and forcing both through one palette optimizes for neither.

Design decisions and rationale. Five decisions shaped the phase. The monitoring agent's escalation ladder was made a set of numeric severity rungs — nominal, advisory, self-heal candidate, and immediate escalation — against fixed drift thresholds, so that the agent classifies a failure against defined boundaries rather than assessing its severity; the rationale is the non-override rule, because a deterministic threshold cannot be softened by a language model's narrative the way an assessed rating could. The Healing Agent was built to repair by cross-domain analogy rather than domain-specific rules: it queries the intelligence layer's cross-domain analogues filtered by failure class and scores the retrieved repair strategies by a function that weights prior success and precondition match, rewards reversibility more than linearly, and penalizes blast radius — the super-linear reversibility preference is a deliberate choice, because the blast radius of an irreversible repair that fails is unbounded.
