The cross-domain sourcing — Medicine, Materials Science, Systems Biology, Military Logistics, and Law — is the intelligence layer's core value, because the same failure class is handled differently in each domain and the analogue score decides which transfer best fits the specific signature; that is the architecture that produces the phase's actual result, a gradual degradation repaired by a homeostatic-smoothing correction drawn from systems biology. The Diagnostic Agent was made permanently read-only, with no write access to any production system, because an auditor's credibility depends on independence from what it audits, and this also enforces the minimum-causal-chain-before-remediation protocol — the Diagnostic must establish why before the Healing Agent is authorized to change anything. And the two decisions about the operator console followed from the palette collision: the stakeholder palette's scope was amended to govern stakeholder artifacts explicitly, the console was exempted and given its own editorial design language, and one additional color — a brick red reserved for the console's critical state alone — was admitted without propagating to any stakeholder artifact, satisfying the red-for-danger requirement for the console without weakening the finding-is-amber convention everywhere else. That exemption came with a full console rewrite, because the original had accreted eleven type sizes and nine weights with no spacing grid, a visual inconsistency that was architectural rather than cosmetic and needed an architectural response — the parchment backgrounds that had made every badge lose its figure-ground separation removed, the type consolidated to five sizes on a strict grid, and all six panels reimplemented.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Three constraints bounded what "autonomous remediation" could mean. The Healing Agent drafts only and never merges: every repair is a draft change staged for review, not a production merge, so remediation in Phase 2 means the agent demonstrates the correct, targeted fix and the audit trail shows why, but a human applies it — "autonomously" describes the reasoning and the repair scripts, not any modification of production data. The Healing Agent escalates to the human only when all six maximum-capacity conditions hold simultaneously — not when two hold, but when all six do at once — with a safety-class bypass for critical, invariant, or audit-trail failures that always escalate regardless, the exception that keeps critical failures from ever being left unattended without loosening the tight escalation rule. And the cross-domain analogues have to be pre-populated: the Healing Agent queries them at repair time rather than at startup, so if the analogue library had been empty before the phase's first run the scoring loop would have found nothing — which makes the intelligence layer both an architectural requirement, continuously running, and a content requirement, populated with the relevant analogues before the agents that depend on them are first exercised.

Lessons learned. Three lessons came out of the phase. The first is that a success state has to be modeled explicitly: the first classifier had no no-failure short-circuit, so after a successful heal the post-verification check returned "below all thresholds," which the classifier read as "no input to classify" and answered with its best guess at a failure class — escalating a fully healed pipeline to the human. Adding an explicit no-failure output at the top of the classifier fixed it, and the lesson generalizes: the absence of failure is itself a signal that needs its own code path. The second is that failure-injection calibration is a discipline rather than a parameter — a structural break at one multiplier sits below the first rung and at a slightly higher one jumps to the top rung, the gradual case demands end values kept within bounds or it becomes a structural break in disguise, and the cascade demands two tables injected at different null rates; each failure class is a distinct signature that has to be engineered faithfully. The third is that cross-table detection belongs at the runner level: giving each agent a single realm preserves its independence and enables running several monitoring instances in parallel later, and the runner-level cascade synthesis is a thin aggregation rather than a new agent — a dedicated cascade-detector agent would have duplicated two monitors' work without adding architectural value.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 2's decisions propagated forward in three ways. The visual-conformance veto built natively into the monitoring agent meant every later phase's stakeholder emissions were checked for off-palette color, generic chart titles, and decorative effects at emission time, so no subsequent phase had to install that check. The cross-domain analogue library seeded here — the five analogue domains with their repair-strategy metadata — is the same library Phase 4's research loop and Phase 5's invention engine would later query, and the cross-domain vocabulary established in Phase 2 was reused throughout. And the operator console's design language, locked in this phase, became the stable foundation for every subsequent interface change, so later refinements added to it without reopening the underlying decisions.

Phase 3 · Experiment analysis and adversarial review

The charter. Phase 3 expanded the Statistician into a full experiment-analysis pipeline and built the Red-Team Agent as a new adversarial capability. Four deliverables — the expanded Statistician, the Red-Team Agent implementing the full twelve-category evasion catalogue, three demonstration experiments, and a stakeholder briefing per experiment — sat against a demanding exit criterion: the system had to identify all three injected pathologies — a sample-ratio mismatch, a novelty effect, and a brittle metric design — without being told which experiment carried which, and the Red-Team had to find the evasion risk before the Statistician issued any ship recommendation.

Engineering challenges. Three challenges defined the phase. The first was calibrating the Red-Team's verdicts against a specific risk the plan names outright: a Red-Team that returns "robust" on every test is not trying hard enough. The Phase 3 problem was the inverse — the first run rated an experiment brittle on generic theoretical concerns about a class of metric, with no experiment-specific evidence — but the naive fix, a prompt clause telling the agent to be less brittle, is itself that named failure mode, because it makes the Red-Team weaker and manufactures false confidence; the right fix was a positive-evidence requirement, treated as a design decision below. The second challenge was that the Storyteller's gates, hardened against the first phase's evidence vocabulary, did not recognize the different vocabulary the experiment evidence carried — statistical-methodology language about data availability, experiment-specific findings, financial-savings phrasing — and it took a chain of seven compatibility fixes before the experiment briefing cleared the L1 layer on its sixth run. Each of those fixes generalized an existing gate rather than adding or weakening one; the principle they express is that a gate should be vocabulary-aware without becoming vocabulary-dependent. The third challenge was ordering: for any experiment the pre-screen flags as ambiguous, the Red-Team has to run before the Statistician, because if the Statistician issues a ship recommendation first the Red-Team is only validating a decision already made rather than informing it — so Phase 3 fixed that ordering as a structural pipeline constraint for pre-screen-flagged experiments.

Design decisions and rationale. Three decisions came out of the phase. The first is the positive-evidence rule for brittle verdicts: a verdict of brittle now has to point to a concrete, experiment-specific attack path rather than a concern that could be raised about any experiment of its type, which preserves the Red-Team's adversarial intensity while requiring evidential grounding — brittle has to mean "I found a specific weakness in this artifact," not "I am uneasy about this class of artifact." Its architectural significance is that it is a deterministic rule applied at the verdict-production step, not a language-model instruction to be more careful, so the Red-Team cannot emit an ungrounded brittle verdict even if its internal reasoning produces one. The second is that the Statistician's mapping from a Red-Team verdict to a ship decision is deterministic — a brittle finding without a sample-ratio problem maps to hold-for-hardening rather than no-ship, because the experiment can be hardened and re-run; a conditionally-robust verdict can still ship if the statistical evidence is clean; and the evasion-hold trigger is scoped to the pre-screen flag rather than a model-only assessment — because verdict-mapping is a governance step, not an analytical one, and leaving it to model judgment would make the map overridable, which the non-override rule forbids. The third is that the Red-Team implements the full twelve-category evasion catalogue rather than a convenient subset, under the completeness directive: if the specification defines twelve categories, all twelve are enforced.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Three constraints shaped the work. The Red-Team had to find the injected brittle design blind — the exit criterion requires it to locate the evasion risk in the relevant experiment without being told which experiment holds it, which is an active test of capability rather than a demonstration of correct behavior on a labeled example. The same risk from the plan bounds it from the other side: the Red-Team has to be strong enough to catch real weaknesses, so it cannot be calibrated toward a comfortable "mostly conditionally robust" default. And a third constraint was self-inflicted and logged as such: one session filled and compacted its context before its mandatory session-end documentation was written — a protocol violation whose structural cause was the six-run, many-call Storyteller compatibility work consuming the window before close. That violation shaped the recovery session that followed and hardened two standing rules, the compaction-override rule and the proactive-context-warning extension, so the same breach could not recur.

Lessons learned. Three lessons stand out. The first is that the operator's rejection of the soften-the-Red-Team proposal was architecturally correct: the calibration clause that was proposed would have made the named failure mode into official policy, and rejecting it forced the positive-evidence solution instead — an instance of the broader principle that when a gate-calibration problem surfaces, the first instinct to relax the gate is almost always wrong, and the right fix is to improve what the gate measures. The second is that phase-to-phase compatibility is a continuous engineering concern rather than a one-time cost: each new phase exercises evidence vocabulary the Storyteller's gates have not seen, and the architecture generalizes the gate vocabulary incrementally rather than spawning a separate Storyteller per phase, which was rejected on parsimony grounds. The third is that experiment analysis exposed the limits of a conditionally-validated verdict: the clean experiment shipped with a caveat that the Statistician's subgroup power was insufficient for small subgroups, and that caveat is exactly what a later phase's telemetry elevated into a structural bottleneck — the Phase 3 Statistician flagged the limitation and the Phase 6 detector elevated it, a continuity that is the operational audit trail working as designed.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 3's work carried forward in three directions. The Red-Team Agent was reused directly for Phase 5's invention stress testing: a new entry point accepts a detection-framework description rather than an experiment, but the adversarial reasoning, the evasion catalogue, and the deterministic pre-screens were already in place, so Phase 5 extended the investment rather than rebuilding it. The Storyteller vocabulary generalizations carried into Phases 4 and 5 without triggering further compatibility fixes, and one of the Phase 4 compounding demonstration's three query classes is experiment analysis, which depends on those generalizations being in place. And the small-subgroup overconfidence first flagged as a known limitation in the clean experiment's statistical result was elevated by Phase 6's telemetry aggregation into the top bottleneck candidate, whose answer is the self-generated Phase 7 proposal — a limitation that took three phases to formally surface, which is the cross-phase audit trail doing exactly what it exists to do.

Sources (Appendix B, Phases 0–3): the build-plan specification with its per-phase objectives, exit criteria, deliverable lists, and risk register; the persistent memory file's architecture-decision, key-finding, and session-history sections; the phase-progression file; the first-investigation postmortem; the change-tracker log; the runtime system prompt and architectural overview; the constraint register; and the agent, library, and orchestration code paths, the semantic layer, the governance configuration, and the artifact and knowledge-vault store. This block covers Phases 0–3; the sources for Phases 4–6 follow below.

Phase 4 · The self-improving cycle

The charter. Phase 4 had to demonstrate that the system learns from its own corrections: that every analyst edit is captured, categorized, and — where it generalizes — folded back into how the agents behave on the next investigation. Six deliverables carried that mandate: a telemetry layer that records each correction, a promotion gate that decides whether a correction is generalizable, a few-shot bank that stores the ones that are, the operationalization of the exploration rule that keeps the system from optimizing itself into a rut, an automated research loop that turns an open question into a web search, and a ten-cycle compounding demonstration to show the whole loop closing on itself. The exit criteria were exacting in a way worth stating precisely: the edit-distance curve had to show a measurable decline for at least two stable query classes, at least one exploration cycle had to surface a non-obvious hypothesis, and the promotion gate had to correctly quarantine at least one ambiguous correction rather than promote it. Learning had to be demonstrated, not asserted.

Engineering challenges. The hardest problem in Phase 4 was demonstrating that the loop compounds without paying for ten live model calls per query class to prove it. The compounding demonstration had to exercise the real telemetry-to-promotion-gate-to-intelligence-layer-to-few-shot-bank pipeline across ten cycles, but ten live calls across three query classes would have been expensive, non-deterministic on re-run, and — the binding constraint — would have consumed the session's context budget the moment the demonstration ran; pure mocks that returned constant output, at the other extreme, would not have exercised the pipeline at all. The resolution was a deterministic stand-in that degrades a canonical, known-good output by a severity that falls as the few-shot bank fills — large when the bank is empty, shrinking with each exemplar retrieved, near-zero once a few are in place — so that each cycle records a real correction triple, runs the real promotion gate, and lets the next cycle retrieve from the now-populated bank. This tests the infrastructure rather than the model's native quality, which is exactly what the exit criterion measures. A second challenge was subtler and more instructive: the first run of the demonstration reported a categorization accuracy of seventeen percent when the true accuracy was fifty — and, after the rule rewrite below, a hundred. The audit harness had paired corrections with decisions positionally, and the two lists were not in the same order, so it was scoring mismatched pairs — a diagnostic that lied about its own pass rate and hid the real, diagnosable floor behind a false one. A third challenge was making the automated research loop testable offline: it triggers external web searches, which are unavailable in test mode, so it had to be built around a pluggable search adapter — an offline stub for smoke tests, an injectable live adapter for production — a pattern that later informed the Phase 6 portability design.

Design decisions and rationale. Five decisions shaped the phase. The first was to accept a deterministic stand-in for the model's compounding behavior as architecturally sound for this purpose, precisely because the exit criterion measures the pipeline's response to compounding correction, not the model's own improvement: the stand-in produces reproducible re-runs, exercises every real pipeline component, and its shaping model — severity falling as the bank fills — faithfully represents what accumulated worked examples do to a real agent's output. The second was structural: after the ordering bug, all audit code from Phase 4 onward pairs corrections with decisions by key rather than by position, a correctness fix that also degrades gracefully as the test set grows, where positional pairing grows more fragile with every added case. The third was the design of the promotion gate itself as a nine-rule categorization that gives strong rule-language signals priority over numerical-token signals — an edit that adds a standing rule ("always start with," "never recommend," "going forward") is by definition generalizable, whereas an edit that only changes a specific number is more ambiguous — and this priority ordering is what carried categorization accuracy from fifty to a hundred percent. The fourth was to make the exploration rule persist across sessions: its cycle counter lives in a state file that survives session boundaries, and its trigger fires whenever the count falls a full cycle below the expected rate, so even a short session advances the counter and eventually forces a backlogged exploration cycle; the analyst may tune the exploration fraction within a bounded band but cannot drive it to zero, because the entire compounding model depends on periodic counter-intuitive hypothesis injection to avoid a capability plateau. And the fifth was to make generalizable-only auto-promotion an invariant: the gate auto-promotes only the clearly generalizable class, routes local exceptions to a separate store, and sends genuinely ambiguous corrections to quarantine rather than to either fate — the direct expression of the proposal-rate-below-review-capacity invariant, because auto-promoting ambiguous edits would fill the operator's review queue with exactly the judgment calls that invariant exists to ration.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Three constraints bounded the work, and the first — the context-budget directive — is what forced the deterministic stand-in into existence: ten live cycles across three query classes plus session overhead would have exceeded the session's context ceiling, so a governance constraint on context, not a modeling preference, produced the testing architecture. The second is that Phase 0's dataset quality is the ceiling on what Phase 4 could show: the build plan warns in as many words that a thin dataset or over-narrow query classes would populate the few-shot bank with trivial corrections and flatten the improvement curve, and that the Phase 0 dataset design is load-bearing for Phase 4. What the ten-cycle demonstration actually measured, stated precisely, is a one-time step reduction in edit distance across the three tracked query classes — API-abuse investigation, experiment analysis, and pipeline diagnosis — concentrated at the point where the first exemplar entered each class's few-shot bank, with the curve flat thereafter through the remaining cycles; that the step was non-trivial rather than negligible is what validated the dataset's signal richness. It is important to be exact about what this does and does not show: the demonstration confirms that the pipeline responds to accumulated corrections, but the further compounding at fifty cycles — a capability that plateaus without the exploration rule versus one that compounds far higher with it — is a specified design target reasoned by cross-domain analogy in the architectural overview, not a measured result of the ten-cycle run, and I mark it as such wherever it appears. The third constraint is that the exploration rule cannot be skipped: the trigger enforces this even across short sessions, because without it the exploration budget would silently degrade to zero in any session too short to reach the tenth cycle, making the rule nominal rather than operational — the tenth-cycle exploration firing on schedule, and surfacing a non-obvious hypothesis from the open constraint register, is the evidence that it holds.

Lessons learned. Three lessons carried forward. The first is that test-harness integrity is a first-class engineering concern, not a supporting detail: a diagnostic that misreports a pass rate is worse than a genuinely low one, because it blocks the fix-and-log loop the whole governance model depends on — the seventeen-percent phantom would have sent debugging in the wrong direction had the fifty-percent real floor not been recovered — and every audit harness in the system now uses key-stable lookups for exactly this reason. The second is that infrastructure testing does not require model calls at all: the compounding pipeline can be exercised end to end with deterministic shaping, the same principle that let Phase 2 inject deterministic drift and Phase 3 inject a deterministic sample-ratio mismatch — reserve the model calls for testing model behavior and test the pipeline with deterministic inputs. The third is that an anti-plateau mechanism has to be enforced by architecture, not by instruction: a system-prompt suggestion to "try a counter-intuitive hypothesis every tenth cycle" would be honored sometimes and skipped others, and the difference between a best-practice guideline and an operational guarantee is precisely the persistent state file, the rate-based trigger, and the floor that cannot be tuned away.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 4's work fed directly into the two phases after it. The few-shot bank it populated — with its agent-scoped retrieval and its prompt-injection path already built — was in place when the Phase 5 invention engine fired and pulled from it during its first calibration run; the invention engine has to know what already exists to judge what counts as new, and the bank is that record. The automated research loop, which generates hypotheses from open constraint-register entries by abduction, cross-domain analogy, and counterfactual reasoning, was the stripped-down predecessor of the Phase 5 engine's full seven-mode reasoning apparatus — it proved that automated, constraint-driven hypothesis generation was architecturally viable before the larger engine was built on the same idea. And the exploration rule Phase 4 established as an operational constant — persistent, session-surviving, rate-triggered — is a load-bearing assumption of the Phase 6 bottleneck analysis, whose self-generated improvement proposal projects its impact on the premise that the exploration cycles are running continuously; the compounding capability-gain design target depends entirely on those cycles being non-skippable, which is why the rule was built to be impossible to disable rather than merely discouraged from disabling.

Phase 5 · The Forge

The charter. Phase 5 built the invention engine — the component meant to produce genuinely new analytical frameworks rather than refine existing ones. Its mandate was complete: a full invention pipeline exercising all seven reasoning modes, a mandatory invention-pipeline report carrying thirteen required assets, persistent tracking of an innovation mandate, and adversarial stress-testing of every framework it produced. Six deliverables carried it, and the exit criteria were the sharpest test of autonomy in the whole build: the engine had to produce a detection framework that was not a refinement of any existing one, that framework had to survive adversarial review at no worse than a conditionally-robust verdict, and all thirteen report assets had to be present — invention had to clear a robustness bar it could not reach by being merely novel.

Engineering challenges. The phase's defining challenge announced itself on the first invention cycle, which produced a framework the adversarial reviewer correctly rated brittle. The engine's model had been handed only the names of the intelligence layer's cross-domain analogues, not their structural content — not the field describing how a pattern in a source domain actually maps onto the analytics target — so it selected an eigenvalue-based spectral approach by name-match and produced something an attacker could defeat by decorrelating their timing slightly, dissolving the signal at almost no cost. The instructive point is that the fix was upstream, not downstream: the reviewer's brittle verdict was right, and the correct response was to give the engine better raw material — the full structural-mapping fields — rather than to soften the reviewer. A second challenge was that the reviewer initially had no vocabulary for the cost of an evasion: "evadable" was binary, either the adversary can defeat the framework or cannot, which collapses the difference between an evasion that costs the attacker nothing and one demanding substantial coordination complexity at a real loss of campaign efficiency. Adding an adversary-cost decomposition — grading coordination complexity and efficiency loss so that a medium-cost evasion yields a conditionally-robust rather than a brittle verdict — is what made the verdicts meaningfully graded rather than a blunt pass/fail, the invention-side counterpart of the positive-evidence precision the reviewer had gained in Phase 3. The third challenge was philosophical before it was technical: how does a system prove novelty with no external oracle to check against? The operational definition it settled on is bounded and honest — a framework is novel if it is not a refinement of any existing metric definition, any prior exemplar in the few-shot bank, or any pattern already recorded in the intelligence layer's surfaced-exemplar index — novelty relative to the system's own knowledge graph, explicitly not an absolute claim of novelty against the field, with a persistent file tracking invention cycles against novel ones.

Design decisions and rationale. Five decisions defined the phase. The first was to pass the full structural content of a cross-domain analogue to the engine's model, not merely its name — a decision about what the intelligence layer is for, because an analogue's name tells the model only that some domain has a relevant pattern, while the structural-mapping field tells it what the mapping actually is, which is the difference between name-dropping and adapting. The second was to require adversary-cost decomposition in every framework verdict, grading coordination complexity and campaign-efficiency loss so that the brittle / conditionally-robust / robust categorization gains cost-of-evasion as a genuine dimension without losing its shape. The third was a pre-screen gate that blocks any brittle framework from ever reaching the operator's confirmation gate, routing it instead to a parked status: the operator cannot be put in the position of approving a framework the reviewer has already shown to be cheaply evaded, so novelty and robustness are enforced together rather than separately. The fourth was to make the innovation mandate a persistent compliance state rather than a per-cycle checkbox — the engine tracks its ratio of novel to total first-principles cycles across sessions and blocks incremental refinement when that ratio falls out of compliance, because without cross-session state the mandate degrades to "this one cycle was novel," which is trivially satisfiable and governance-meaningless. And the fifth was to require all thirteen invention-report assets on every cycle regardless of outcome — even when the reviewer rates the framework brittle and the pre-screen gate parks it — because the assets exist to create a complete audit trail of the invention reasoning, the reasoning behind a failure included, which the completeness and summary directives demand as forcefully here as anywhere else in the system.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Three constraints bounded the work. The first is the same minimum-strength requirement that governed the Phase 3 adversarial reviewer, applied here with equal force: a reviewer that returns conditionally-robust on every invention is not trying hard enough, and every novel-but-unexamined framework would then advance toward shadow deployment carrying unseen weaknesses — the first cycle's brittle verdict was the reviewer behaving correctly, and the fix was richer engine context, never a softer reviewer. The second is that the Phase 4 few-shot bank had to be populated before the engine could run at all, because the novelty determination is defined relative to what already exists: an empty bank leaves the engine with nothing to innovate beyond, so Phase 4's completion and the exemplars it accumulated were a hard prerequisite. The third is the any-idea-needs-approval directive: the invention engine itself was specified rather than improvised, but its implementation details — how to structure the pipeline, how to operationalize the novelty test, how to pass the intelligence-layer context — required explicit sign-off wherever a design choice was not already fixed by the specification.

Lessons learned. Three lessons stand out, and the first is the clearest demonstration in the whole build of what the intelligence layer is worth: the first cycle's brittle framework was not caused by a weak model but by insufficient context, and the same model given full structural mappings produced a structurally grounded framework — the layer does not generate the ideas, but it determines whether the ideas the model generates are grounded or name-matched. The second is that adversary cost is a distinct concept from adversary possibility, and a framework evadable at zero cost is categorically different from one evadable only at significant cost; the binary verdict collapses that distinction, and the cost decomposition is what restores it. The third is that the pre-screen gate has to block before the confirmation gate, not after: routing a brittle framework onward for operator review is not a safe fallback but an unsafe one, because it asks the operator to vet something already shown to be weak — the parked status is the correct architectural response, letting the system generate proposals freely while ensuring a brittle one can never be submitted for approval.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 5's outputs propagated into Phase 6 on three tracks. The validated invention it produced once the engine had full structural context — the Spectral Coordination Sieve, which cleared adversarial review at a conditionally-robust verdict — was stored both in the intelligence layer's surfaced-exemplar index and in the invention vault, and Phase 6's routing later classified it as stakeholder-briefing material, confirming that the routing logic correctly distinguished a novel invention from a routine operational output. The adversary-cost vocabulary established here became available to Phase 6's improvement-proposal generator, so that any proposal which would lower adversary cost for an existing detection approach is evaluated in the same graded terms. And the engine's persistent compliance-state file is a concrete instance of the session-spanning state architecture Phase 6's bottleneck detector depends on — telemetry that survives session boundaries is precisely what makes aggregated analysis across all prior sessions possible.

Phase 6 · Full AIMS and recursive self-improvement

The charter. Phase 6 had to bring the whole system together: a complete automated-intelligence routing layer classifying every output to its correct destination, and a functioning recursive self-improvement loop that could find its own weakest point and propose a fix. Five deliverables carried it — the full routing layer, a bottleneck-identification pass over the system's own accumulated telemetry, an improvement proposal with a sandbox test, a stakeholder briefing for that proposal, and the portability layer that would let the system move to another model provider without a rebuild. The exit criteria asked for something the earlier phases had only approached: a full workflow running without human scaffolding at any intermediate step, the human gates working correctly at the one place a human belongs, and a portability wrapper both documented and functional. This is the phase where autonomy and governance had to hold at the same time.

Engineering challenges. Three challenges defined the phase. The first was an immutability violation caught by the very rule it violated: the Orchestrator assembled a capability bundle, sealed its content hash at creation, and then mutated one field with a value that only became available after the intelligence-layer query had run — and because the audit-trail-completeness invariant requires every artifact's content hash to be stable from emission onward, the mismatch was caught at write time rather than surfacing later as a silent corruption. The fix was not merely to patch it but to understand its cause: the mutated value had to be computed before the hash was sealed, which meant resolving the cycle-counter logic earlier in the method so that all content fields are assembled before creation. The second challenge was routing determinism at scale: the demonstration audited 175 artifacts across all six phases, split 89 to the operational log and 86 to stakeholder briefings, and every one of the eighteen-plus artifact types had to be classified correctly by deterministic logic — any model involvement in routing would have made routing overridable, which the non-override invariant forbids, so the routing had to match the specification's routing table exactly with no model in the loop. The third challenge was the safety of the self-improvement loop itself: the loop can generate proposals freely, bottom-up from telemetry to bottleneck detection to a drafted improvement, and the engineering problem was to guarantee it can never self-approve — which was solved by making the confirmation-gate routing for a self-generated proposal structurally identical to the routing for a first-phase investigation, the same no-auto-approve rule, the same awaiting-decision status, the same audit entry, so the loop's safety comes entirely from the governance invariants and not from limiting what the system is allowed to propose.

Design decisions and rationale. Five decisions shaped the phase. The first was that routing is deterministic logic, not model classification — a dictionary lookup from artifact type to destination, using the same rules the specification documents — because model-assessed routing could produce different results for the same artifact type in different sessions, whereas deterministic routing lets the audit trail for any artifact be reconstructed from its type alone. The second was that bottleneck detection works by aggregating the system's own telemetry across every prior phase rather than by the operator nominating likely problem areas: the top candidate — the Statistician's overconfidence on small subgroups — emerged at eighty-three percent confidence from the aggregated pattern, having been flagged as a limitation in multiple earlier statistical results, and that it emerged from the data rather than from a hunch is what validates the continuously-running intelligence-layer architecture chosen back in Phase 0. The third was that adopting a self-generated proposal requires operator sign-off, without exception: the improvement the loop produced — a minimum-sample-size guard with an exact-method substitution — passed sandbox testing five times out of five and was ready to deploy, and it was nonetheless not deployed but routed to the confirmation gate as submitted and awaiting decision, because the no-auto-approve rule applies to a self-generated proposal exactly as it applies to any consequential action. This is the principled line between recursive self-improvement and unsafe self-modification: the loop is bounded not by limiting what it can propose but by requiring human authorization for every adoption, and the one proposal currently sitting at the gate is not an unfinished task but the clearest possible evidence that the rule holds. The fourth was to treat the portability layer as documentation of three integration points rather than a second provider migration — the surfaces a future migration would actually have to address, namely tool-format differences, context-window limits, and extended-thinking availability — because the wrapper's value is its stable interface, and documenting the seams before any migration pressure is cheap where discovering them mid-migration is expensive. And the fifth was a small but telling interface decision: the streaming variant of the model call returns the same result dictionary as the synchronous one, so that consumers which do not need streaming never have to branch on it — the contract is "give me a result," and whether it arrives streamed or whole is an implementation detail the consumer should not have to know.

Constraints that shaped the phase. Three constraints bounded what the self-improvement loop could be. The no-auto-approve rule and the proposal-rate-below-capacity invariant together define its operational boundary: the first prevents adoption without review, the second prevents the loop from generating faster than the one operator can review, and together they license unlimited generation, gated adoption, and a capacity-throttled proposal rate — the loop is free to think and constrained only at the point of consequence. The second constraint is that content-hash immutability catches its own violations precisely because it is enforced at creation rather than at some later audit: had the rule been advisory — a warning logged on a hash mismatch — the Phase 6 mutation would have stayed invisible until a much later replay, and the fact that the rule surfaced its own violation immediately is what makes the audit trail trustworthy rather than merely present. The third is that the portability wrapper, though only documented as load-bearing in Phase 6, had to be respected from Phase 1: every model call in all six phases went through the wrapper's single generate interface, so that Phase 6's portability work made an existing interface explicit rather than retrofitting one that had never been maintained.

Lessons learned. Four lessons close the phase. The first is that a write-after-hash mutation is an architecture smell wherever it appears — any method that creates an object with a sealed attribute, receives a value back from that creation, and then modifies the object with that value is a latent violation — and the correct pattern, computing all content before creation, eliminates the entire class rather than the single instance. The second is that telemetry aggregation is only as good as the log persistence it aggregates: the bottleneck detector could assemble its eighty-three-percent candidate only because every phase from the second onward had written consistent operational logs to the same structure and the intelligence layer had maintained state across all those sessions — the Phase 6 result retroactively validates every Phase 0 decision that kept the audit trail complete. The third is that the safety of recursive self-improvement is architectural, not behavioral: a loop told not to self-approve is subject to model reasoning that might find a reason to; a loop that routes to a gate enforcing no-auto-approve at the infrastructure level cannot self-approve regardless of what the model reasons — the same principle that has governed every deterministic veto since Phase 1. And the fourth is that the portability wrapper pays for itself at migration time: the three integration points documented here are the actual surface a provider change would confront, and a modest block of documentation written before any migration pressure is an insurance premium against an expensive mid-migration discovery.

Cross-phase influence. Phase 6 closed the loops the earlier phases had opened. Its routing audit at scale confirmed that the routing logic set down in the specification is operationally complete — no artifact type needed special-case handling and the audit found zero misrouted artifacts — a validation that reaches back retroactively over every prior phase's emissions. Its bottleneck detector identified the small-subgroup overconfidence that traces to a limitation first documented in a Phase 3 experiment, and the self-generated proposal is the system's answer to a weakness that took three phases to formally surface: the recursive loop working as designed, an audit trail from Phase 3 becoming the evidence base for a later improvement proposal. And the portability documentation is the bridge to production beyond this build: when the system eventually moves from its generated-Parquet and DuckDB simulation stack to a BigQuery warehouse layer, the wrapper's generate interface is the one surface that has to stay stable while everything else changes around it — the reason the interface was made load-bearing from the first phase rather than the last.

Cross-phase synthesis

Seen whole, the seven-phase build has an internal logic that only becomes visible in retrospect: each phase's hardest engineering problems were not caused by that phase's new features but by the foundations of prior phases meeting a new requirement for the first time. The Phase 1 Storyteller calibration — 18 development runs to clear three deterministic gates — was Phase 0's abstract system-prompt instructions meeting the first live model output, and the fix was worked examples, a Phase 0 retrospective. The Phase 2 cascade-detection calibration was the failure-injection parameters meeting the monitoring agent's drift thresholds for the first time, and the fix was a recalibration of Phase 0's dataset-injection design — another Phase 0 retrospective. The Phase 3 adversarial-reviewer calibration was the reviewer's generic-concern template meeting the requirement for experiment-specific evidence, and the fix — a positive-evidence rule — validated the risk-register warning written in Phase 0. Phase 5's first-cycle brittle verdict was the invention engine's context being names-only rather than structural mappings, a Phase 0 content-quality retrospective. And Phase 6's content-hash mismatch was the Orchestrator's post-call mutation meeting Phase 0's immutability rule for the first time in a multi-step compute path. The pattern is consistent: Phase 0 established the invariants, each later phase generated the first use case that violated one of them in a non-obvious way, and the fix-and-log directive turned each violation into a lasting architectural improvement rather than a patched symptom. What held all of this together was the governance framework itself — the fix-and-log mandate that prevented any "known but not fixed" backlog from accumulating, the deterministic vetoes that kept governance from becoming advisory, the no-auto-approve rule that kept the confirmation gate from becoming a rubber stamp. The twelve Design Invariants are locked not because they were obvious at the outset — several took multiple phases to demonstrate their necessity — but because the build itself revealed, phase by phase, exactly how load-bearing each of them is.

C Appendix C · Performance comparison evidence A single governed investigation compresses a two-to-five analyst-day workflow into 288.9 seconds — with citation coverage enforced mechanically, not aspirationally

A first-person benchmarking record — the performance-comparison evidence behind Topic 12 (Performance Metrics) and Topic 3 (Business Value). It opens with the headline finding and how the comparison was built, walks ten evidence dimensions (efficiency, throughput, quality, consistency, scalability, time savings, compounding knowledge assets, organization-wide composite lift, cross-departmental impact, and the non-obvious conclusions), and closes with a weighted blended performance multiplier and a financial-outcomes model. Every claim carries one of three labels — [Measured] (observed in a validated simulation run), [Benchmarked] (a named external industry figure), or [Projected] (a model built on stated assumptions) — and no assertion is left unlabeled.

A single governed investigation compresses a two-to-five analyst-day workflow into 288.9 seconds of wall-clock time — and does it with its governance intact: the released report's 94.6% citation coverage, enforced by three deterministic vetoes that cannot be overridden.

The architecture is also designed to compound. At fifty cycles its specified design target diverges from a traditional workflow at a rate well beyond the plateau a system without a forcing function for exploration would reach — but that magnitude is illustrated by cross-domain analogy, not yet validated. The ten-cycle demonstration confirmed only that the improvement pipeline fires correctly: a one-time forty-to-fifty-three-percent edit-distance reduction as the first exemplar entered each query class, then flat. I keep the compounding magnitude labeled as a design target everywhere it appears, because that is what it is.

I want to be precise about how this comparison was built, because its honesty is part of its value. No direct A/B trial against a human analyst was run on the same question — that experiment does not exist in this build. What follows draws on Maldros-validated simulation data, the architecture's own benchmark figures, and named external industry sources, and every claim is labeled by exactly how it was derived: where a number is measured I point to the run that produced it, where it is an industry benchmark I name the source, and where it is a projection I state its assumptions.

Impact · Why the advantage is not primarily about speed

The speed is real and measured, but three properties matter more than it does.

The quality guarantees are mechanical, not aspirational. Three deterministic vetoes — one against unsupported causal language, one against uncited claims, one against omitted material findings — fire at the lowest layer of the inference stack and cannot be overridden by the language model or by me. A human analyst working under deadline cannot replicate a floor that fires without exception; the value is not a lower average error rate but a bounded one.

The institutional knowledge compounds rather than decays. Every investigation strengthens the knowledge vault, the Few-Shot Bank, and the cross-domain intelligence index. A human analyst's tacit knowledge walks out the door at resignation; the system's accumulates permanently and is available to the next investigation regardless of who runs it.

The compounding figure is a specified design target — not a projection from thin air, and not a measured magnitude. The ten-cycle demonstration validated that the improvement pipeline fires correctly (that one-time forty-to-fifty-three-percent edit-distance reduction across three query classes, then flat); the fifty-cycle target is grounded in a hard-coded architectural rule — a ten-percent exploration budget the system cannot skip — with documented analogues in immune-system biology, self-play reinforcement learning, and endogenous-growth economics. The mechanism is validated; the magnitude is a design target, and I label it as one everywhere it appears.

Evidence 1 · Efficiency: time per investigation

[Measured] The Phase 1 end-to-end investigation — Orchestrator, Analyst, Statistician, and Storyteller in sequence — completed in 288.9 seconds of wall-clock time. That figure covers the whole arc: hypothesis formation, data analysis across 750,000 API-event records, statistical validation, and generation of the stakeholder-briefing report. The elapsed time is recorded in the operational log under a traceable run identifier.

[Measured] The Phase 6 end-to-end audit completed in 73.6 seconds, auditing 175 artifacts at 100% routing accuracy.

[Benchmarked] The architecture's own estimate for the classical human equivalent of an investigation of this type is two to five analyst-days, with the analyst's active time under Maldros (review and approval only) at fifteen to thirty minutes per investigation. Independent industry data is consistent with that human baseline: the Turning Numbers 2025 fraud-investigation benchmark reports that under sixty percent of internal fraud-investigation teams close cases within thirty days, and coordinated-abuse cases of the kind Maldros investigated routinely run longer than that window.

[Projected] At fifteen to thirty minutes of analyst active time per Maldros investigation against an estimated fourteen to twenty analyst-hours for a comparable human-led fraud investigation (derived from the two-to-five-day benchmark at fifty-to-sixty-percent utilization), the system delivers roughly a 28–80× reduction in analyst active-time per investigation. The projection is deliberately conservative: it excludes the coordination overhead, meeting time, and context-switching costs of a human-led workflow.

Evidence 2 · Throughput: analyses completed per run

[Measured] Phase 6 audited 175 real artifacts in a single run at 100% routing accuracy — 89 operational-log items and 86 stakeholder briefings, correctly separated. That volume would represent weeks of human analyst output.

[Measured] The Phase 3 experiment analysis processed three experiments blind, producing a correct no-ship verdict (a sample-ratio mismatch it detected), a correct hold-for-hardening verdict (a Brittle Red-Team finding plus a novelty effect), and a correct ship verdict (Conditionally Robust) — without being told in advance which pathology each experiment carried.

[Benchmarked] Industry surveys of analytics-team throughput treat question-to-decision turnaround as the primary throughput metric; the ACFE 2025 benchmarking report documents fraud investigators carrying fewer than five open cases at a time, which implies roughly one substantiated closure per week per investigator for complex cases. Maldros is not rate-limited the same way — its throughput ceiling is compute and context, not analyst bandwidth.

Evidence 3 · Quality: citation coverage and governance-compliance rate

[Measured] The Storyteller's final validated Phase 1 run reached 94.6% citation coverage — 88 of 93 factual claims fully attributed — under the three deterministic vetoes: a causal-language veto (no causal assertion without causal evidence upstream), a citation-coverage veto (the report is blocked if any claim is unattributed), and an omission audit (the report is blocked if any material finding is missing).

[Benchmarked] Research on human reviewer error rates in systematic analytical reviews documents an average 10.76% error rate across 139,467 citations (a PLOS One study). For financial-analytics reporting, the industry-standard "acceptable" error rate is cited at five percent or below, with best-in-class organizations targeting under one percent. Maldros's 2.8% uncovered rate sits above the "acceptable" threshold — and, more to the point, the three vetoes mean any deviation below the required floor blocks the report rather than shipping it with errors.

[Projected] A human analyst producing 107 factual claims in a complex fraud report under time pressure would statistically expect eleven or more attribution errors at that 10.76% benchmark. The governance value is not merely a lower error rate; it is that the system's error rate is bounded by a deterministic floor that fires without exception, while a human's is variable and pressure-dependent.

Evidence 4 · Consistency: deterministic versus variable output

[Measured] Across the Phase 1 Storyteller iteration log, the vetoes fired consistently across the 18 development runs on the same underlying evidence — 14 of them blocked — producing the same block-or-pass decision regardless of run order or prompt variation. The blocked runs stayed blocked until the governance criteria were actually satisfied.

[Measured] The Confirmation Gate enforced its no-auto-approve rule across every test — the Phase 0 functional test, the Phase 1 sign-off, and the Phase 7 proposal. The gate entry for the Phase 7 proposal reads, in as many words: this proposal does not deploy until the operator explicitly approves it; silence is not approval; timeout is not approval.

[Benchmarked] Research on organizational knowledge consistency finds that when personnel change, 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the departing individual and is unavailable to successors until it is painstakingly reconstructed — the consistency risk no training program fully closes.

Evidence 5 · Scalability: structural advantages over a human-led workflow

[Measured] The Phase 4 self-improvement demonstration ran ten improvement cycles and measured a one-time edit-distance step reduction — roughly forty to fifty-three percent — across all three tracked query classes (coordinated-abuse investigation, experiment analysis, and pipeline diagnosis) as the first exemplar entered the Few-Shot Bank, then flat through the remaining cycles. That is the improvement pipeline firing correctly, not a decline curve. I want to be exact about what this measures: edit-distance here is a word-level text-similarity score between a deterministically simulated output and a hard-coded per-class canonical target, not a live model call, and the step shape follows directly from the simulation's manually set degradation-severity map. The result validates the capture-and-propagate mechanism; it carries no independent dollar or productivity value on its own and does not establish that a live agent's output improves by this magnitude — the full mechanical definition is in Topic 12. On schedule, the exploration-budget rule fired at the tenth cycle against the least-used open hypothesis in the constraint register, surfacing a counter-intuitive line of inquiry the system currently disbelieves.

[Measured] Phase 5 — The Forge — produced the Spectral Coordination Sieve, a genuinely novel detection framework generated from first-principles reasoning with no prior template, which passed adversarial Red-Team stress testing at a Conditionally Robust verdict. This is a capability class that compounds in value: a novel framework persists in the knowledge vault and the intelligence index, available to every later investigation rather than locked in one analyst's memory.

[Projected] A traditional analytics workflow scales by hiring — each hire needing three to six months of ramp, carrying non-transferable tacit knowledge, and introducing key-person dependency. Maldros scales by adding investigations to the queue; the knowledge layer grows with each one without additional headcount.

Evidence 6 · Time savings: quantified from validated run times

[Measured] The Phase 1 pipeline ran Orchestrator, then Analyst, then Statistician, then Storyteller, to a 288.9-second total, with per-agent timings recorded in the operational log.

[Measured + Benchmarked] In Phase 2 self-healing, three injected failure classes were each remediated in a single attempt with a passing verification result. The DORA 2024 research benchmarks elite engineering teams at a mean-time-to-restore under sixty minutes for production incidents, against low performers above twenty-four hours; Maldros's autonomous detection and single-attempt remediation removes the detection lag, triage overhead, and on-call escalation entirely for recognized failure classes.

[Benchmarked] Undetected pipeline failures cost an organization roughly $190 per minute of downtime for a hundred-million-dollar-revenue business (PagerDuty/Splunk MTTR benchmarks). At a two-hour manual resolution time for a recognized failure class, that is about $22,800 per incident in direct revenue impact alone — before analyst time, downstream data-quality effects, and cascading errors from stale data.

Evidence 7 · Organization-wide strength: compounding knowledge assets

[Measured] The knowledge vault (a linked markdown corpus with a vector index), the cross-domain intelligence index (continuously updated across eight knowledge domains), and the Few-Shot Bank (generalizable corrections auto-promoted from telemetry) are persistent across sessions and personnel changes. Every operational-log and stakeholder-briefing entry, every promotion-gate decision, every healing record, and every discovery report is written immutably with a full provenance chain.

[Measured + Projected] The Phase 4 demonstration measured the improvement pipeline firing correctly — that one-time forty-to-fifty-three-percent edit-distance reduction across three query classes, then flat [Measured]. The forward divergence figure — a marked capability gain at fifty cycles with the exploration rule against a plateau without it — is a specified design target [Projected], illustrated by cross-domain analogy, not derived from the ten-cycle run and not yet validated in magnitude. The trajectory it describes is a design consequence of the Few-Shot Bank and the intelligence index accumulating non-obviously useful exemplars from exploration cycles.

[Benchmarked] Large US companies lose an average of $47 million a year in productivity to inefficient knowledge sharing alone; with 42% of institutional knowledge unique to the individual, a senior analyst's exit costs successors direct access to nearly half of the judgment patterns that analyst carried. The vault-and-index architecture is a direct architectural countermeasure to that class of organizational risk.

Evidence 9 · Cross-departmental impact

Each department below draws value from a different architectural feature, so the gains do not compete for a shared benefit.

Product. Maldros delivers statistically grounded, Red-Team-validated ship/no-ship recommendations with full methodology disclosure. The Phase 3 demonstration caught a sample-ratio mismatch in a no-ship verdict and a novelty effect in a hold-for-hardening verdict without being briefed on the injected pathology. [Measured] Wrong shipping decisions in A/B experimentation routinely produce product debt, rollback cost, and user-experience damage an order of magnitude larger than the investigation itself. [Benchmarked, Turning Numbers 2025 and the pricing-experiment literature]

Finance. The Phase 1 investigation attributed $5.89M in Q1 financial impact from API abuse across the US and EU and identified the 41-account coordinated cluster responsible for the concentration — actionable at the countermeasure level, not merely descriptive. [Measured] The causal-language veto keeps financial projections from being overclaimed: the system cannot ship an estimate labeled causal without causal evidence upstream, which directly reduces exposure-quantification errors that would otherwise need correction cycles.

Legal/Compliance. Three deterministic vetoes fire on every Storyteller run, and every artifact carries a full provenance chain, a content hash, and an immutable version history, making any finding replayable and defensible. The average cost of a compliance-failure event is cited at $14.82M against $5.47M for proactive compliance infrastructure [Benchmarked] — a 2.7× ratio before counting regulatory-penalty risk (GDPR fines starting at $11M or 2% of annual revenue). The audit trail is not a feature bolted on top; it is the foundational architecture.

Engineering. Pipeline self-healing at the two lowest severity rungs eliminates the detection-to-triage-to-resolution cycle for recognized failure classes. Phase 2 demonstrated detection, classification, and remediation in single attempts across a structural break, a gradual degradation, and a cascade. [Measured] Incident-response downtime costs $190-plus per minute at scale [Benchmarked]; the autonomous response removes the human-in-the-loop latency for a class of failures that would otherwise require on-call escalation.

Executive/Strategy. Stakeholder briefings are dual-layer by design — a plain-language executive summary followed by full technical depth — and every one requires human sign-off before action under the no-auto-approve invariant. Executives receive findings framed as conclusions with financial-exposure estimates, not raw data requiring synthesis, and without depending on analyst availability at the moment a decision is needed.

Public Policy. Policy teams at AI companies need to quantify harm — abuse rates, financial impact, evasion patterns — for regulators who will scrutinize methodology. Maldros produces exactly that artifact class: methodology-documented, causally conservative (the causal-language veto blocks overclaimed assertions), and source-cited. [Measured: causal-language veto and methodology-disclosed briefings] Cross-referencing the regulatory-events feed against the internal signal timeline enables a capability most policy teams lack — detecting whether internal abuse-pattern changes preceded or followed regulatory events, which is material for regulatory defense and proactive filing. [Design-complete]

Go-to-market / Sales. The same statistical-validation pipeline that stress-tests fraud-detection frameworks can stress-test a market-sizing model or a customer-cohort claim. GTM analyses often rest on segment comparisons that are effectively A/B tests, subject to the same sample-ratio-mismatch risk the Phase 3 demonstration caught blind. [Measured] The counterfactual-simulation reasoning mode addresses a core GTM question directly — "if we had made this pricing change last quarter, what would the revenue impact have been?" [Design-complete] A strategy deck backed by Red-Team-validated analysis carries different credibility in a board or customer conversation than one produced under analyst time pressure without a quality gate.

Trust & Safety. This is the highest-specificity application of the core investigative capability. The Phase 1 coordination-detection methodology — graph connectivity plus entropy asymmetry, separating coordinated clusters from organic volume — transfers directly to real T&S work. More important, The Forge produces detection frameworks that do not exist yet: the Spectral Coordination Sieve was generated with no prior template and passed Red-Team stress testing at Conditionally Robust. [Measured] T&S's core challenge is adversarial adaptation — threat actors evolve faster than static frameworks — and a system that invents novel detection frameworks faster than actors can invalidate existing ones is categorically different from one that applies known frameworks faster. The twelve Red-Team evasion categories are built specifically for adversarial-actor scenarios. [Measured] Transfer caveat: the methodology was validated on synthetic fraud data; transfer to real T&S data is integration work, not architectural work — the mechanism is domain-agnostic, the specific signal assumptions are not.

Model Safety. The synthetic dataset's API-event table, with its legitimate/borderline/policy-violation content categories, is structurally identical to a real model-output log carrying a safety classifier. The Phase 1 question — "is this rate spike coordinated adversarial behavior or organic distribution shift?" — translates verbatim to model-safety monitoring. [Measured mechanism; Projected transfer] Population-stability drift detection (Phase 2) applies directly to safety-relevant output distributions over time. [Measured] The Bayesian-updating reasoning mode addresses model safety's specific statistical challenge: rare safety failures accumulate slowly, and you want to surface them above a probability threshold before a hard threshold is crossed, not after. [Design-complete] Architecturally, the deterministic L1 checks that cannot be overridden by the language-model layer are an exact analogue for the model-safety problem of holding hard behavioral floors that survive distributional shift.

Evidence 10 · Other findings: non-obvious conclusions

The governance architecture has indirect economic value that throughput metrics do not capture. The three Storyteller vetoes fired and blocked 14 of the 18 Phase 1 Storyteller runs during development, before any run met all three governance criteria. [Measured] Those were build-time iterations rather than intercepted production releases, so the measured fact is the behaviour of the gate, not a count of averted incidents: no draft that failed a check reached me for review, because enforcement is deterministic and sits upstream of human review rather than after it. In a production compliance context that same mechanism is what would keep a non-compliant report from being released at all.

The Confirmation Gate's no-auto-approve rule is already proven under the hardest condition: the system testing its own proposal. The Phase 7 self-generated improvement proposal — a minimum-N guard for small-subgroup analyses — is sitting at the Confirmation Gate awaiting human sign-off. [Measured] The system correctly intercepted its own proposal, logged it, and blocked deployment pending explicit operator approval. This is not a bug or a limitation; it is the governance invariant working exactly as designed. An organization deploying a self-improving AI system without this gate faces uncontrolled model drift — Maldros demonstrates the countermeasure working in practice.

The specified capability divergence — a design target, not yet validated in magnitude — is about more than analytical quality; it is about staying ahead of adversarial actors. In fraud and abuse, threat actors improve over time. A system that plateaus (the no-exploration branch of the design target) is progressively outpaced by evolving attack patterns; a system that keeps compounding can keep surfacing novel detection frameworks (like the Spectral Coordination Sieve) faster than actors can invalidate them. The mechanism that drives this — the non-disableable exploration rule — is built and validated at the pipeline level; the fifty-cycle magnitude is a specified target, not a measured one. [design target; Projected]

The one area where human judgment remains irreplaceable is trust. A named constraint in the register explicitly makes external relationship-building a permanent human-only function. Maldros produces the artifacts and recommendations; it cannot hold the cross-functional relationships that determine whether those recommendations are acted on. That asymmetry should shape deployment: Maldros is a capability multiplier for human analysts who retain stakeholder-relationship ownership, not a replacement for the human-facing function.

Recommendation

For technical evaluators. The most important performance signal in this comparison is the measured governance-intact speed result — a full governed investigation in 288.9 seconds with citation coverage mechanically enforced on the released report (three vetoes, 14 of 18 development runs blocked, a traceable run identifier), reinforced at scale by the Phase 6 audit (175 artifacts, 100% routing, 73.6 seconds, one Confirmation Gate intercept). Evaluate that first: it is verifiable against the artifact logs today. The compounding architecture is the second signal and a genuine differentiator — the improvement is tied to an exploration rule the system cannot disable — but its fifty-cycle magnitude, the design target, is specified, not yet validated; the ten-cycle demonstration validated the mechanism, not the magnitude. Most analytical AI systems plateau because they have no equivalent forcing function for exploration; assess competing systems on whether they enforce governance mechanically and whether they carry such a mechanism at all.

For business evaluators. Anchor the ROI case on governance-compliance risk reduction and institutional-memory retention, not throughput alone. The compliance-failure cost differential ($14.82M against $5.47M, a 2.7× ratio) means a single prevented failure event pays for significant analytical infrastructure. The 42% knowledge cliff on analyst departure is a systemic organizational risk that Maldros addresses architecturally rather than through process or training.

For organizations considering deployment. The current build status is single-operator simulation on a synthetic dataset. These figures are validated on that foundation, not in a live production environment. The path to production is an integration task — swap the data sources — not an architectural rebuild, but that step matters for resetting baseline expectations appropriately.

Sources (Appendix C, Part 1 — FINDING through RECOMMENDATION, evidence dimensions 1–10): the operational-log records for the Phase 1 investigation, Phase 2 self-healing, the Confirmation Gate, the exploration-rule firing, and the promotion gate; the architectural overview (the compounding design target and the human-equivalent workload estimate); the persistent memory file's Verified Source Facts; and named external industry benchmarks — the ACFE 2025 and Turning Numbers 2025 fraud-investigation reports, a PLOS One human-citation-error study, the DORA 2024 incident-response research, PagerDuty/Splunk MTTR benchmarks, a 2026 compliance-cost analysis, and organizational knowledge-loss research. Every claim is labeled [Measured], [Benchmarked], or [Projected]; the exact internal identifiers are kept in the internal record. The weighted blended multiplier and the financial-outcomes model, with their own sources, close the appendix below.

§11 · Weighted across all eight dimensions, the blended multiplier is 12.8×–38.3× — situating the 28–80× anchor, not replacing it

The 28–80× cycle-time figure from Evidence 1 is the single strongest anchor in this appendix, and I keep it as the headline. This section answers a different question: taken across all eight dimensions of analytical work at once — not cycle time alone — how much more productive is one unit of analyst capacity under Maldros than under a traditional workflow? The weighted blended multiplier is my synthesis answer. It is deliberately a lower number than the 28–80× peak, and it should be — it is a capacity-weighted average that folds the dimensions where the improvement is modest (quality at 1.99×, consistency near 1.5×) in with the ones where it is large. Its purpose is not to replace the headline anchor but to situate it.

§11.1 · Completing the inventory — four dimensions not yet given an explicit multiplier

Four of the eight dimensions were covered qualitatively in earlier sections but never given an explicit function-level multiplier. I complete the inventory here, before the blended calculation, because a weighted average is only as honest as the completeness of the terms feeding it.

Throughput — investigations per unit of analyst resource. A single analyst running complex coordinated-abuse investigations manages roughly four to six per quarter at full utilization: the ACFE 2025 benchmarking report documents thirty-day closure for under sixty percent of fraud-investigation teams, and complex coordinated cases routinely run longer, so at fourteen to twenty active analyst-hours each against a realistic sixty-to-eighty-hour quarterly pool, four to six is the ceiling. Under Maldros, at fifteen to thirty minutes of analyst active time per investigation, that same pool could in principle oversee 120 to 320 investigations a quarter — bounded in practice by question identification and prioritization, not execution. My conservative operational estimate, carrying the overhead of question formulation and review scheduling, is 24 to 48 investigations per quarter at the same headcount: a 6–16× throughput multiplier [Projected]. The active-time figure is [Benchmarked] from the architecture's operator-interface timing spec, the per-analyst ceiling is [Benchmarked] from ACFE 2025, and the multiplier is a projection off those two benchmarks — no parallel-throughput experiment was run.

Scalability — unit cost per investigation as volume rises. At the reference traditional workflow — a $525K fully-loaded team against twenty investigations a year — a human-led investigation costs $26,250 per investigation-unit, and scaling volume forces additional headcount that pushes that unit cost onto a non-linear curve. Maldros inverts the curve: its cost is a fixed platform-engineering and integration base with near-zero marginal compute, so unit cost falls as volume rises. At the concurrent frontier scale modeled in §12.1, Layer-A cash cost divided by annual volume runs ~$300 per investigation at ~750/year, ~$112 at ~3,900/year, and ~$49 at ~15,000/year [Projected] — against the $26,250 human unit, a raw unit-cost efficiency of roughly 88× to 536× that widens with scale. I deliberately do not carry that raw figure into the blended multiplier below: for §11.3 I cap scalability at a conservative 18–62× band, because a single volume-amortization dimension should not dominate a capacity-weighted average meant to characterize typical per-investigation capability lift, not peak cost-efficiency at maximum concurrency. The label is [Projected]: unit cost is modeled from the §12.1 cost structure, not production billing.

Labor utilization — the value-adding fraction of the analyst's day. Knowledge-worker research consistently finds analysts spend only 35–45% of working time on core value-adding analysis, the rest lost to coordination, status meetings, documentation formatting, tool-switching, and waiting on upstream data — I take 40% as a conservative baseline (McKinsey Global Institute knowledge-worker productivity analysis, cited via iteratorshq.com 2026; RescueTime time-use research). Under Maldros the analyst's fifteen-to-thirty-minute contribution per investigation is by construction almost entirely value-adding — reviewing conclusions, signing off on governance, applying contextual judgment — while data gathering, hypothesis generation, statistical validation, QA, and formatting all run in the agent pipeline. I estimate the value-adding fraction rises to 70–80% [Projected], a 1.75–2.0× improvement [Benchmarked + Projected]. The ceiling is deliberately honest: the remaining 20–30% is exactly the work Maldros does not touch — team coordination, roadmap, and the external stakeholder relationships that a named constraint in the register makes permanently human-only. This is a different measurement from Evidence 1: that section compresses the time one investigation takes; labor utilization captures how the analyst's whole day is then spent.

Decision-making effectiveness — time to a defensible, decision-ready output. A complex fraud investigation under a human-led workflow runs two to five active work-days, plus half a day to a day and a half drafting the executive briefing, plus QA and iteration — a stakeholder-ready briefing in three to seven calendar days, at a quality that varies with analyst availability and load (Heap.io/Coalesce.io analytics-throughput research treats time-to-decision as the primary throughput metric). The Maldros pipeline — Orchestrator, Analyst, Statistician, Storyteller — generates the dual-layer briefing, technical layer plus plain-language executive summary, in 288.9 seconds [Measured]; with fifteen to thirty minutes of analyst review, a defensible decision-ready output exists within hours of the question, not days. And the quality holds: Phase 3's blind experiment analysis returned 3/3 correct verdicts with no advance knowledge of the injected pathology [Measured], and the released briefing carries 94.6% citation coverage under three deterministic vetoes [Measured]. On the wall-clock, two analyst-days against 288.9 seconds is a 200× compression; the more honest calendar-time framing — a Monday question a human workflow delivers Thursday, Maldros the same day — is 5–6× [Projected], and I use that conservative 5–6× figure (not the 200×) as the anchor in the blended calculation, with 5–24× as the full range. The label mix is [Measured] for the 288.9-second run and the Phase 3 accuracy, [Benchmarked] for the two-to-five-day human baseline, and [Projected] for the calendar-time compression the simulation did not measure.

A note on knowledge compounding. This is the one time-dependent dimension in the table. At initiation the compounding advantage is 1.0× — no cycles have run. The relative advantage develops over fifty investigation cycles, and — holding to how I label it everywhere in this case study — the fifty-cycle magnitude is a specified design target reasoned by cross-domain analogy, not a measured result; what the ten-cycle demonstration actually measured was the one-time edit-distance step as the first exemplar entered each query class, then flat. For the blended calculation below I therefore use a conservative 1.2× (early cycles), a base 3.0× (twenty-plus cycles), and reserve the full fifty-cycle design-target magnitude for the optimistic case only.

§11.3 · Weighting by operational hours consumed, the blend computes to 12.8× / 24.6× / 38.3×

Weighting basis: operational hours consumed in a traditional workflow. I weight each dimension by the fraction of an analyst's active working time it represents in a traditional (non-Maldros) investigation — the more time a dimension consumes, the more weight it carries — because that directly reflects where analyst capacity actually goes. The weights are derived from general knowledge-worker time-use research (McKinsey, RescueTime) applied to a complex-analytics context; they are estimates, not measured from any specific employer's workflow data.

The formula is a straightforward weighted average, Blended = Σ(weight × multiplier) — an arithmetic mean of the individual-dimension multipliers weighted by time share, producing an overall capacity-weighted productivity figure. Across all three weighting methodologies and all three scenarios, the blended multiplier lands in the range 7.9×–49×. The spread is driven mostly by how heavily cycle time is weighted — it has both the largest individual multiplier (28–80×) and the largest time share in traditional workflows. The result is methodologically stable: Maldros delivers a material blended advantage under every weighting approach, from 7.9× (equal weights, conservative) to 49× (dollar-value weighted, optimistic).
