§12 · The financial model, rebuilt for concurrent frontier scale: the binding cost is the platform-engineering headcount to operate the system, and value scales from the Evidence 8 building block

Evidence 8 gave the value side of the composite at a single-organization reference scale. This section adds the cost side and the financial metrics that fall out of putting the two together — ROI, payback period, enterprise value, and margin impact — but rebuilt for the usage shape a frontier AI company actually has: concurrent, many analyst seats at once, on a production-integrated system rather than a single-operator script. The cost side (§12.1) is modeled in two honest layers — incremental cash (Layer A) and reallocated oversight (Layer B) — across three concurrent seat scenarios (15 / 30 / 60 seats → ~750 / ~3,900 / ~15,000 investigations a year) on multi-billion-ARR reference organizations. The value side keeps the Evidence 8 six-component decomposition intact as the per-unit building block and scales it to the concurrent organization by seat count and revenue base, with explicit diminishing returns — never by naive volume multiplication. Every input is labeled [Measured], [Benchmarked], or [Projected], and simulation-baseline figures (DuckDB, sequential runner) are shown beside production-target figures (BigQuery, parallel runner) so the reader can see what is built and what is designed.

§12.1 · At concurrent frontier scale, incremental cash cost runs ~$210K–$800K a year — dominated by the platform-engineering headcount to operate the system, not by tokens or warehouse

Why this section was rebuilt. The earlier version of this model measured a single operator running twenty investigations a year, and reported an all-in figure of a few thousand dollars. That is the honest number for the simulation as it was built — but it is not the number a frontier AI company would budget, because the real usage shape at that scale is concurrent: many analyst seats running investigations at the same time, against a production-integrated system rather than a single-operator script. Re-modeled at that scale, the cost splits into two layers the single-operator figure conflated.

Layer A — incremental cash cost is net-new spend the organization would not otherwise incur: API tokens, warehouse queries, runner infrastructure, amortized production-integration, and the platform-engineering headcount to keep the system running. Layer B — analyst oversight is reallocated existing capacity, not net-new cash: it is the same analyst time Evidence 8 already credits as freed capacity on the value side, so booking it again as a cost would double-count. Layer B is therefore shown separately, below Layer A, never added into the cash-cost line — which preserves this case study’s locked framing of Maldros as a capability multiplier, not a headcount replacement.

The impact of the two-layer split: once the platform-engineering headcount is surfaced honestly, the binding cost of running Maldros at scale is people to operate it and one-time integration — not marginal compute. Tokens and warehouse, the line items intuition expects to dominate an “AI system,” are together under ten percent of incremental spend at every scenario.

Concurrent seat scenarios [Projected assumption]. Frontier labs are smaller than the general-technology sector but run on far higher revenue-per-employee (~$5M+), with a lean trust-and-safety / fraud-and-risk / analytics-investigation function. “Investigation seats” is that cross-functional analyst subset — a labeled modeling assumption, not a measured headcount. Cadence is bounded by question formulation, not execution, since analyst active time per investigation is only fifteen to thirty minutes.

Volume = seats × cadence (~50 / ~130 / ~250 investigations per seat-year). Peak concurrency is the worst case in which every seat fires at once; average concurrency is far lower. Peak is what the design-target parallel runner must serve — the sequential build cannot (Layer A(c)). [Projected]

(Fast-mode processing runs higher; batch submission and prompt caching run lower.) Notably this is lower than the retired model’s $7–$18 per investigation, which was built on an older, higher-priced model tier — an honest downward update, not a discount.

Unit cost falls as concurrent volume rises. Layer-A cash ÷ annual volume gives ~$300 per investigation at Conservative scale, ~$112 at Base, and ~$49 at Aggressive — unit cost declines with scale, because the platform-engineering and integration cost is fixed while tokens and warehouse are near-zero marginal. Recommendation. Budget Maldros at production scale as a platform-engineering line, not a compute line: the binding costs are the operating headcount and the one-time integration, and the parallel-runner seam must be built before peak concurrency can be served. Read against the value side (§12.2) and the multi-billion-ARR reference org (§12.5), a $210K–$800K incremental cash cost is a small fraction of both the value delivered and the organization’s analytics budget — but it is an honest six-figure number, not the few-thousand-dollar figure a single-operator simulation produces.

§12.2 · ROI runs ~45:1 to ~50:1 on the general composite — a lower, more defensible band than the single-operator model, and the cost of running the system still is not the binding constraint

Formula: ROI = (annual value delivered − annual Layer-A cash cost) / annual Layer-A cash cost. Value is the Evidence 8 composite scaled to the concurrent organization by the per-component drivers introduced in §12; cost is the Layer-A incremental cash from §12.1. The finance component is shown separately, for organizations with material fraud or abuse exposure.

The scaling keeps Evidence 8 intact as the per-unit building block. Seat-driven components (AE direct, capacity expansion, Product, Executive) scale with analyst seat count; the two finding-value components (AE capacity expansion, Product) carry an explicit concave, diminishing-returns curve; the revenue/exposure components (Compliance, Engineering, Finance) scale sub-linearly with the multi-billion-ARR base — never by naive investigation-volume multiplication. Sensitivity — applying the same drivers to Evidence 8’s conservative and optimistic columns widens the general composite to roughly $5.5M–$22M (Conservative), $9.4M–$38M (Base), and $16M–$65M (Aggressive); the base-column figures above are the midpoint. All figures [Projected].

A framing note on the ROI ratios. The ratios are still high, but this is a lower and more defensible band than a naive scaling would produce — because value is scaled from Evidence 8 by explicit per-component drivers with diminishing returns, never by naive investigation-volume multiplication (which at this scale would multiply value by 195× and produce indefensible absolutes). The honest executive framing is unchanged: the cost of operating Maldros is not the binding constraint — production integration, governance, and question formulation are.

§12.3 · Payback lands in days — the one-time production-integration cost against a far larger monthly net value

Formula: payback = one-time production-integration cost / monthly net value, where monthly net value = (scaled annual general composite − annual Layer-A cash cost) / 12. The one-time production-integration cost is the ~$150K–$330K per scenario carried in §12.1 (before three-year amortization).

Payback period by concurrent scenario
ScenarioOne-time integrationMonthly net value (general)Payback
Conservative (15 seats)~$150K($11.6M − $225K) / 12 = ~$945K/mo~5 days
Base (30 seats)~$225K($20.0M − $435K) / 12 = ~$1.63M/mo~4 days
Aggressive (60 seats)~$330K($33.8M − $735K) / 12 = ~$2.76M/mo~4 days

These payback periods are the mathematical consequence of a small one-time integration cost against a large monthly net value; they are not a claim of instant value. In practice, value realization ramps over the first one to three months as the knowledge vault and intelligence index accumulate operational context and the pipeline reaches consistent performance. The right reading is that Maldros is not a capital-recovery problem — production integration and governance-workflow establishment are the relevant early-stage milestones. [Projected]

§12.4 · At 5–10× multiples the scaled annual value capitalizes to ~$58M–$338M (general) — a capitalization framing, not a valuation of the software

This framing treats the scaled annual value stream as a revenue-equivalent asset valued at a market multiple — a financial exercise for board and strategic-planning audiences, not a valuation claim for the Maldros software itself.

Revenue-multiple references [Benchmarked]: horizontal analytics tooling comparables run 5–8× ARR; vertical enterprise-grade AI-automation platforms run 8–15× ARR; fraud-specific analytics / fintech risk runs 10–15× ARR (Palantir/Verafin comps). I use 5–10× as the conservative-to-base multiple range.

General composite (no finance component)
ScenarioScaled annual value5× EV10× EV
Conservative (15 seats)$11.6M$58M$116M

Aggressive (60 seats)$33.8M$169M$338M
With finance component (fraud-domain organizations)

Conservative (15 seats)$22.2M$111M$222M

These figures are the capitalized present value of the scaled annual value stream — what an acquirer might pay for a comparable analytics-automation capability at current market multiples — not a valuation of the software product or any implied transaction. Applying the system’s specified compounding trajectory (a design target by cross-domain analogy, not a measured magnitude) would raise these further; that projection carries [Projected] status throughout and is deliberately not shown as a headline figure, because it rests on the specified design target, not a measured magnitude.

§12.5 · On a multi-billion-ARR base the value is 0.2–0.4 margin points — smaller than at $200M scale, because the impact now spreads across a far larger revenue base; the ROI and freed-capacity story carries the weight

Scaled annual value as a fraction of revenue on the multi-billion-ARR reference organizations. The margin-point impact is honestly smaller than at the retired $200M-ARR reference — not because the value is smaller (it is far larger in absolute terms) but because it now sits on a revenue base ten to seventy times bigger.

Margin-point impact by concurrent scenario
ScenarioARR anchorScaled general valueMargin points (general)With finance
Conservative (15 seats)~$3B$11.6M0.39 margin points0.74 margin points
Base (30 seats)~$8B$20.0M0.25 margin points0.47 margin points
Aggressive (60 seats)~$15B$33.8M0.23 margin points0.41 margin points

ARR anchors are labeled [Projected] reference points for the three frontier-org scales; margin points = scaled value ÷ ARR.

Why the frame shifts at scale. At $200M ARR a few million dollars of value was a visible one-to-three margin points; at multi-billion ARR the same class of value is a fraction of a point, so margin-point impact is the wrong headline. The right frame at frontier scale is capability and cost-efficiency: a ~45:1 general ROI and a unit cost that falls to ~$49 per investigation (§11.1, §12.1), delivered without adding analyst headcount.

Freed capacity, at scale. The mechanism is unchanged from Evidence 8, only larger: 14–20 analyst-hours of investigation mechanics freed per investigation × concurrent volume. At the Base scenario that is roughly 55,000–78,000 analyst-hours a year redirected from execution to question formulation, stakeholder engagement, and the external trust-relationship work a named constraint in the register keeps permanently human-only. This is why the case study frames Maldros as a capability multiplier for the human analytics function, not a headcount reduction — the freed hours are redirected, not eliminated. [Projected]
